subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT THAT HIS MAJESTY WILL, ACCREDIT A CANADIAN PLENIPOTENTIARY TO THE UNITED STATES.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Rt, Hon. Sir GEORGE FOSTER (Acting Prime Minister): Mr. Speaker, I desire

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
to make a statement which, from the importance of its character, I shall read, with the permission of the House. It has reference to negotiations which have for some time been going on between the British and the Canadian Governments in Tespect of Canadian representation at Washington. The negotiations have been concluded, and to-day a statement will have been made in the House of Commons in London, and I desire that the House of Commons here shall have cognizance of the matter at the same time.
As a result of recent discussions an arrangement has been concluded between the British and Canadian Governments to provide more complete representation at Washington of Canadian interests than has hitherto existed. Accordingly, it has been agreed that His Majesty, on advice of his Canadian ministers, shall appoint a Minister Plenipotentiary who will fiave charge of Canadian affairs and will at all times be the ordinary channel of communication with the United States Government in matters of purely Canadian concern, acting upon instructions from and reporting direct to the Canadian Government. In the absence of the Ambassador the Canadian minister will take charge of the whole Embassy and of the representation of Imperial as well as Canadian interests. He will be accredited by His Majesty to the President with the necessary powers for the purpose.
This new arrangement will not denote any departure either on the part of the British Government or of the Canadian Government from the principle of the diplomatic unity of the British Empire.
The need for this important step has been fully realized by both Governments for some time. For a good many years there has been direct communication between Washington and Ottawa, but the constantly increasing importance of Canadian interests in the United States has made it apparent that Canada should be represented there in some distinctive manner, for this would doubtless tend to expedite negotiations, and naturally first-hand acquaintance with Canadian conditions would promote good understanding. In view of the peculiarly close relations that have always existed between the people of Canada and those of the United States, it is confidently expected as well that this new step will have the very desirable result of maintaining and strengthening the friendly relations and cooperation between the British Empire and the United States.

maintopic: RETIREMENT OF CERTAIN MEMBERS OF PUBLIC SERVICE.
speechtext: This Bill is very similar to one which was introduced, if I am not mistaken, at the session before last. Resolved, That it is expedient to repeal the Acts relating to the Harbour of Piotou, in the province of Nova Scotia, and to transfer the property, rights and assets now held by the Harbour Commissioners to His Majesty in the right of Canada, and to provide that His Majesty shall assume and discharge all the obligations and liabilities of the said commissioners.
Will the minister kindly explain the purpose of this resolution.

Its object is to permit of the introduction of a Bill to permit of the transfer of the Harbour of Pic-tou, Nova Scotia, from the Department of Marine to me Department of Public Works. The reason for the transfer is that the revenue of Pictou Harbour is less than the expenditures in connection with it. The revenue for the seven years from 1913 to 1919, inclusive, amounted to $3,388, whereas the expenditure was $3,840. While the harbour is under a Harbour Commission, no moneys can be spent to repair the wharfs there unless the revenue permits of that being done; but the committee will notice that according to the figures I have given the expenditure during the period referred to has been greater than the revenue. The commission is unable to make the necessary repairs to the wharf as matters stand, and therefore it is proposed-if hon. gentlemen agree to the present resolution and to the Bill which is to be based upon it- that the harbour shall be transferred from the Department of Marine to the Department of Public Works.
speakername: Mr.   B A L L AN TYNE@

speechtext: What has been the yearly revenue from the wharfs in question and what property is it proposed to repair?

The revenue is derived from what is known as wharfage dues and the revenue for the past seven years

has been as follows: 1913, $678; 1914, $789; 1915, $999; 1916, $356; 1917, $253; 1918, $151; 1919, $162. Hon. members will notice that there has been a gradual decrease in the receipts year by year and that in 1919 the revenue amounted to only $162, and in 1918 to $151. Under present conditions there is no opportunity to repair any of the Government wharfs at Pictou. If the hon. member for that constituency (Mr. McGregor) is in the House he will be in a position to give more detailed information upon the subject.
speakername: Mr.   B A L L AN TYNE@

speechtext: I would like to know if the wharfs from which this revenue is derived are Government wharfs or private wharfs; also what liabilities the Government have to assume in connection with this transfer?

The Department of Public works built the wharfs many years ago. I find that the first Harbour Commission was appointed in the year 1873. The commission is composed of Mr. D. Sutherland, chairman, (appointed October 19, 1912), and Messrs. Thomas Caqlie, Hugh Murray, William Fraser and George H. Macdonald.
Wharves are usually built by the Department olf Public Works and then transferred to the Department of Marine. In this case the local board has been collecting the dues and doing the necessary repairs since 1873. Owing to the decline of business the revenue has been decreasing, and I am informed that the necessary repairs cannot now be taken care of by the revenue. The Department of Marine has not the necessary authority to attend to the work, but the Department of Public Works could do so if the committee passes this resolution.
speakername: Mr.   B A L L AN TYNE@

speechtext: What is the cause of the decline in revenue from year to year?

It will be noticed by the figures given by the minister that the revenue collected previous to the war was quite considerable, but during recent years it has fallen off to practically nothing, and consequently the Harbour Commission is not able to maintain the three wharves in repair. These wharves will come under the control of the Public Works .Department if this Bill passes. I may say that the commissioners have always given their services gratuitously, being public-spirited citizens. The expenditure in future will be greater by reason of the fact that a large amount [DOT]of money has been spent by the Public Works Department in deepening and straightening the channel of the East
river to Trenton and New Glasgow and constructing locks, and it is in the public interest that this work should 'be taken care of by the Public Works Department.

Were these wharves built
by the Government?
Yes.
What are the liabilities that the Government have to take over?

So far as I know
the Public Works Department will not take over any liabilities. The sole object of the resolution and of the Bill based upon it is that the necessary repairs may be made by the Public Works Department. If the Marine Department had the necessary authority to do these repairs, of course, I would not be asking hon. members to pass this resolution. But I think the committee will agree that an important babour like Pictou must be kept up, and it cannot be unless the proposed transfer is made.
speakername: Mr.   B A L L AN TYNE@

speechtext:
My only reason for asking is that the resolution states:
and to provide that His Majesty shall assume and discharge all the obligations and liabilities of the said commissioners.
As regards the Government taking over the property, I think it is the right and proper thing to do, and I have no objection to this course being taken; all I am asking for is information before the resolution is passed, and I think I aim entitled to such information.

The hon. member
has all the information that the Government is in possession of. This is simply a transfer of the harbour to the Public Works Department, and I am not aware that there are any liabilities to be assumed.
IMr. LEMIEUX:	While I do not object
to this resolution, I must say that there are other wharves, and piers, and docks in the Dominion which have been absolutely ignored for the last eight or ten years. I refer particularly to such works built on the Baie de Chaleur (and on the 'St. Lawrence; many of such wharves and piers have been damaged by storms and not one dollar's worth of repairs made. Speaking for my own constituency, I for one do not ask the Government to spend any money on those works, for 'I realize that the country is passing through a great financial crisis, and in view of the heavy taxation which is impending it is the desire of every man and woman that any heavy commitments should be very seriously considered

by the Government before they are undertaken. Since the beginning of the war public works from Halifax to Vancouver have been built which, having regard to our tremendous financial obligations, might well have been delayed. I need not name any of those public works, but they are to be found in every province. With the very heavy tax bills which await them the electors will not stand for any but absolutely urgent expenditure on piers, wharves or docks for the next few years, and I hope when those expenditures are proposed to t'he Minister of Finance in council that he will blue-pencil any which are not absolutely necessary. I could give a long list of public wharves built by the Government which were very useful to our fishing population, but which have been completely abandoned,-particularly when they were situated in constituencies represented by members of the Opposition. But under the circumstances I do not begrudge the refusal of the Government to meet our requests for repairs to those public works. However, I appeal to my hon. friend the Acting Prime Minister (Sir George Foster) not to commit the country to any nonurgent expenditure while every elector is expecting the visit of the tax collector with heavy demands to meet the huge debt which confronts this country.
speakername: Mr.   B A L L AN TYNE@

speechtext: I wish to assure the hon. member (Mr. Letmieux) that the Government have no intention of constructing new wharves or of spending large sums of money at the harbour of Pictou. In proof of that I might say that the new Estimates do not contain one single dollar for this harbour. The Government would be at perfect liberty to repair the harbours to which my hon. friend refers, but so far as Pictou is concerned, even if the wharves were falling to pieces the Pictou Harbour Commissioners have not the necessary revenue which would enable them to effect repairs, and the Department of Marine have no authority to spend money other than what is derived from the harbour dues, and so on. I am merely asking that this transfer be made; I want to make it plain that it is not the intention of the Government to spend any large sum of money on Pictou harbour.
speakername: Mr.   B A L L AN TYNE@

speechtext:
The minister says that no liabilities are being assumed by the Government in this respect. If there are obligations or liabilities, why say in the resolution :
And to provide that His Majesty shall assume and discharge all the obligations and liabilities of the said commissioners.

This is merely legal phraseology; the transfer is provided of the liabilities from the local harbour board to His Majesty. I have been informed by the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. McGregor) that there are no current liabilities.
speakername: Mr.   B A L L AN TYNE@

speechtext: What amounts are paid out by the Harbour Commission for salaries?
The only money that is expended is $200 a year to the harbour master. The harbour commissioners give their services gratuitously.
speakername: Mr.   B A L L AN TYNE@

speechtext: I would suggest that the liabilities referred to in this resolution include liabilities incurred through neglect on the part of the Government to keep the harbour in a proper state of repair.

I am glad that the harbour of Pictou is so fully qualified to become Government property. The wharves are falling to pieces; the revenue is not nearly equal to the expenditure, and the minister evidently has found the conditions to be such that the property should be acquired by the Government. I would like to know whether a report has been made with regard to this matter, either to the minister or to the Department of Public Works. Let me tell the minister at once that I am in favour of the public ownership of harbours. The harbours of Sydney and North Sydney are now free ports; ships coming in have nothing to pay; no- harbour dues are collected. When the transfer which this resolution proposes has been effected, will the harbour dues no longer be payable in the harbour of Pictou? I should like to know also whether this change has been made at the request of the Harbour Commissioner's. In connection with the harbour of North Sydney the authority of the commission was simply cancelled and in that way the properties were vested in the Government. The harbour master at that port is a Government official; he looks after -ships which do business in the harbour. But -at North Sydney any obligation o.f the oommision was looked after by themselves; no obligations were assumed by the Government except the future obligation of effecting the necessary improvements and repairs. If similar conditions are to apply to the harbour of Pictou and the property i-s transferred to the Government free from obligation, I have no objection to 'the proposal; I think it is a step in advance.

We want to do the same with Pictou as was done with North-

Sydney. The port is now in possession of His Majesty, the Harbour Commissioners being merely trustees or managers. The object of the resolution is to do away with the commission and to make Bi'etou a free harbour. The Harbour Commissioners waited upon the Government some time ago and urged that this 'be done.
speakername: Mr.   B A L L AN TYNE@

speechtext: Are any 'bonds or other liabilities outstanding against the harbour?
I had a careful investigation made before proposing the resolution. There are no liabilities whatever.
speakername: Mr.   B A L L AN TYNE@

speechtext: When the minister says that ilt is proposed to make Pictou a free harbour, does he mean that wharfage dues will no longer be collected, that sick mariners' dues will not be charged, and that the ordinary expenses of shipping which apply at other ports will not apply at Pictou?
As soon as this transfer is made, no wharfage dues will be charged alt Pictou. Siok mariners' dues, which are separately covered by statute, will etoll be charged.
speakername: Mr.   B A L L AN TYNE@

speechtext: Why make a difference between Pictou harbour and other harbours and wharves? As I understand the matter, when the Public Works Department builds a wharf at any point, that wharf is handed over for management and collection of dues to the Department of Marine, and apparently that has been done in this case. When, however the question of expenditure is involved or when it is proposed to make a wharf free, it is handed back to the Department of Public Works. What led the Government to come to the conclusion that this wharf in preference to others should be free and should be handed back to the Department of Public Works for maintenance when other wharves have to pay wharfage dues?

Generally speaking, wharves throughout Canada are not only constructed by the Department of Public Works but maintained under that department except where there is a good deal of shipping. The large ports of Montreal, Vancouver, Quebec, have, of course harbour commissions which administer the ports lor the Crown. Then there are smaller ports similar to Pictou, at which there has beer a good deal of shipping, gnd it has been the custom for many years for the Department of Public Works to transfer such wharves to the Department of Marine. Had the
shipping at Pictou harbour kept up and the revenue likewise kept up, I would not be asking hon. members now to pass this resolution. I would not want to convey to the committee the impression that the wharves at Pictou harbour are in a dilapidated condition. They are, I am informed, in very good condition but some repairs will have to be made probably next year, and the revenue has not been sufficient to pay even the harbourmaster who draws a salary oi $200 a year. There would not be a twenty-five cent piece left out of revenue for repairs, and in the public interest, if repairs are necessary, they ought to be done at the expense of the public. There is nothing now in the Estimates for repairs to this harbour, but next year or some other year there may be, and, therefore, I am asking the transfer to be made now.
speakername: Mr.   B A L L AN TYNE@

speechtext:
I have in mind some
wharves on the Timiskaming lakes, which wharves are in charge of the Marine Department which collects wharfage dues there. I want to know why this particular dock is picked out as one for special treatment as against wharves on smaller lakes and inland waters where the farmers have to pay charges for the privileges of taking their goods over the docks both in shipping the goods out and in shipping them in. For instance, at Haileybury and Ville Marie the farmers have to pay dues for the privilege oi shipping their hay over the docks to the market; they have no railroad, and they tell me that in the last few years they have been suffering quite a hardship in having to pay what they consider very high wharfage charges at those points.

If the condition of the wharf to which my hon. friend refers is such that it needs repairs and the revenue is not sufficient to cover the cost of making those repairs, then it would be quite in order for the hon. member to ask whatever Government happened to be in power at the time, to make a transfer, the same as I am asking now. There is, however, 4 p.m. a difference between local wharves as compared with an important harbour such as Pictou. I have been informed that $1,000,000 has been spent on Pictou harbour; that there are large and important locks there, to look after which engineers are required, and the rev-'enue does not permit of that. I am quite sure the hon. member would not want an expenditure that has been made, amounting now to $1,000,000, not to be properly looked after. The harbour commissioners

have not -revenue enough to do the work; the Department of Marine has not the authority to do it, and I hope hon. members will agree with me that this transfer is not going to mean any very heavy additional expense to the country.
speakername: Mr.   B A L L AN TYNE@

speechtext:
The wharf to which I refer has a larger revenue than the wharf about which the minister is speaking, and I am-sure the people there deserve just the same treatment as the people at Pictou or at any other place. In fact, they deserve perhaps a little better treatment because they are pioneers opening up a new country. Has the Government any set plan as to how these different wharves throughout the country are administered and why should they select one particular wharf for special treatment? Is it the policy of the Government that when a wharf becomes dilapidated under the administration of the Marine Department to transfer it back to the Public Works Department, and then when repairs are made, to transfer it back agaii to the Marine Department?
Mr. BALLAlNTYNE: The general policy is that wharves at which there is any large quantity of shipping, are transferred to the Department of Marine. In the case of Haileybury wharf, I should understand from the remarks of my hon. friend that the revenue is quite sufficient to keep that wharf in a proper state of repair. But supposing, for argument's sake, that were not so, it would be quite in order for the Minister of Marine to ask that that wharf be transferred from the Marine Department to the Public Works Department. If the revenue had kept up at Pictou harbour the same as it has apparently kept up at Haileybury harbour, I should not be asking that this resolution pass.
How many harbour commissioners are there at Pictou and by whom are they appointed?

The Governor in
Council appoints the harbour commissioners. The following harbour commissioners were appointed on October 19, 1912; Mr. D. Sutherland, chairman; Mr. Thomas Cantley, Mr. Hugh Murray, Captain William Fraser and George H. Macdonald. None of these five commissioners receive any remuneration.
speakername: Mr.   B A L L AN TYNE@

speechtext:
According to the wording of this resolution, I understand this commission exists by virtue of a statute and that the minister is now asking for the repeal of that statute. These commissioners
[Mr. Ballantyne.l
who administer the harbour of Pictou are appointed under this particular law which created the harbour of Pictou. Is it the intention of the minister hereafter to have some employees of his department or another commission or somebody else look after the harbour, because after this commission goes out of existence, there will be nobody to look after the harbour except the Department of Marine.

When this resolution and the Bill founded on it are passed, the responsibility of the harbour of Pictou is transferred from the Marine Department to the Public Works Department, and the Public Works Department, I am informed, already have engineers at Pictou who would have to take on the additional duty of looking after the locks and wharves there. speakername: Mr.   B A L L AN TYNE@

speechtext:
The resolution does not seem to be very well worded. It reads:
Resolved, that it is expedient to repeal the Acts relating to the harbour of Pictou, in the province of Nova Scotia, and to transfer tne property, rights and assets now held fcy the harbour commissioners to His Majesty in the right of Canada, and to provide that His Majesty shall assume and discharge all the obligations and liabilities of the said commissioners.
Does that mean, according to my hon. friend, that after the transfer of the property to the Minister of Public Works, the Minister of Public Works will simply carry on the usual work of administering that property and repairing it, or does it mean something more, namely, that according to the language used in the resolution, there are really liabilities? And to provide that His Majesty shall assume and discharge all the obligations and liabilities of the said commissioners.
The minister, of course, states that a rigid inspection has taken place under the direction of some officer of his department, and that he has personal knowledge that there are no liabilities at all to be assumed by the Government.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: This resolution has been passed upon by parliamentary counsel, and I must accept his phraseology and defer to his knowledge in the matter. The commissioners are going to be relieved of all their authority and henceforth the responsibility will, be vested in the Minister of Public Works.

According to the inspection of the books made by my hon. friend's officers there are no liabilities as implied in the words of the resolution. The meaning of the word "liabilities" is generally understood.

Before the resolution carries I should like to have it distinctly understood in what sense the harbour of Pictou will be free when the Bill which is to be based upon the resolution becomes law. I should not like the plain unqualified statement to reach the shipping men that the harbour is going to be free. In my opinion, if the resolution and the subsequent Bill are passed, the shippers of goods in Pictou harbour will have to pay the same wharfage dues as do people who use any other public wharves in Canada. The same applies to ships going in or out of Pictou harbour. They will have to pay the same pilotage dues as ships in other parts of the country, so the same harbour dues and all other fees so that in these respects Pictou harbour will not be any different from other ports in Canada.
That is right
speakername: Mr.   B A L L AN TYNE@

speechtext:
I wonder if my hon.
friend would submit the report which the accountant made in regard to the books of the Harbour Commission of Pictou. I am always afraid of assuming new liabilities. I have recently passed St. John, N.B., which is a great city that I much admire. I remember some years ago the Government assumed the liabilities and obligations of the harbour of St. John, and they proved very heavy indeed; and although I do not imagine that the same huge expenditure will be made in the harbour of Pictou, yet I am always suspicious of any future or past liabilities assumed by the Government in regard to harbours. As I say, I have just seen St. John and I can guess how many millions were sunk in the Bay of Fundy, and I should not like to assume responsibilities of the same proportions in connection with any other harbour in Canada.
If it is the pleasure of the committee to pass this resolution, I shall be very glad, when we are in committee on the Bill, to give all the assets and liabilities in detail.
speakername: Mr.   B A L L AN TYNE@

speechtext:
As I understand any
schedule of tolls for the harbour, and all dues, dockage, moorage, etc., are to be submitted to the Minister of Marine, and these are to be subject to his approval. I understand from the minister that the Harbour
Commission is to go out of existence and that the harbour will come under the control of the Department of Public Works. How is it to be administered? It is not the intention to re-appoint the commission there. The harbour at Pictou will be under the Department of Public Works just like hundreds of other harbours throughout Canada. The only important change that will be made will be in regard to wharfage dues, or, as some people call them, "top" wharfage dues, which will disappear with the local harbour commission itself. The responsibility for the harbour and the property of the Crown in connection therewith will rest entirely with the Minister of Public Works, and as the Department of Public Works has local engineers down there now no additional expenditures will be entailed. It will simply mean a little more work for the engineers of the Department of Public Works located at Pictou; they, instead of the local harbour board, will have to look after the harbour, the locks and piers.
speakername: Mr.   B A L L AN TYNE@

speechtext:
Do I understand that
there will be no more harbour dues on steamers going to Pictou and that the port will be free.

It will be a free
port in the sense indicated my the hon. member (Mr. Duff). The pilotage dues and sick mariners' dues will be charged, but the small fees levied on the cargoes of ships inbound and outbound will be abolished.
speakername: Mr.   B A L L AN TYNE@

speechtext:
Does the minister say
that in future his policy will be to hand over to the Public Works Department the properties of any harbours which are in financial difficulties?

That will be the
policy of the Government.
speakername: Mr.   B A L L AN TYNE@

speechtext:
I think the minister
will wisely come to the conclusion that it is small business to collect dues from these wharves in different parts of the country. I remember well, many years before the minister came into the House, when a Bill was passed by which these wharves were to be taken over by the Marine Department and dues were to be charged. There was a vigorous opposition to the Bill and it

was only by reason of the fact that it was a Government measure under a minister who is now a judge of the Supreme Court, the Hon. Mr. Brodeur, that it was passed. But there was never any other opinion than that these wharves were built for the public convenience of people who as a rule are located in isolated places where, unless there were wharves, they could not get any benefit from passing ships. For many years the Government had no intention whatever of making any charge. It is quite proper of course that there should be a man to look after the wharves and to see that they do not fall into disrepair, but it is not worth while for any Government to collect these small fees that are charged. The minister is going to abolish the system in Pictou, and the sooner he applies it to the other harbours of the same class the better. Pictou harbour is an important one. In my own county there are many harbours that are not under the control of the board but they have Government wharves which are indispensable; and the policy inaugurated within the last few years of collecting wharfage in these places is in my opinion highly undesirable. I trust that the policy to be established in regard to Pictou harbour will extend to every other place in Nova Scotia where there are public wharves on which fees are now collected.	.

speechtext:
The House resumed from May 4 consideration in committee of Bill No. 57 (from the Senate) to amend the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act, 1907-Hon. Mr. Meighen-Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 2-signatures requisite for applications to refer disputes to boards and for statutory declarations accompanying them:

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The reason for the adjournment of this clause was the calling the attention of the committee by the hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) to the amendment of 1910 and to the fact that that evidently was overlooked in the preparation of this Bill. That is quite correct and it should not have been overlooked. It is the intention of the Minister of Labour that clause 3 of the amendment

of 1910, which is the clause referred to by the leader of the Opposition, shall still be law. I therefore beg to move:
That clause 2 be amended by adding thereto the following after the word "Act" in the first line thereof the following:
"As amended by section 3 of chapter 29 of the statutes of 1910."
That is the part that repeals section 3 of the statutes of 1910.
And by changing the semicolon at the end of subclause (b) thereof to a period; and by adding to paragraph (d) of the new section 16 the following words:
"Where a dispute directly affects employees in more than one province, and such employees are members of a trade union having a general committee authorized to carry on negotiations in disputes between employers and employees, and so recognized by the employers, may be signed by the chairman or president, and by the secretary of the said committee."
These words sought to be added by the -amendment are the exact words that are inserted by section 3 of the amendment of 1910.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Before this
clause as amended carries I should like once again to direct the minister's attention to the effect of the changes he is proposing as to the manner in which the application shall be made for a board of conciliation and investigation under this Act. The minister has made a change, at the suggestion of the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. McDonald) in regard to subsection (d). If he is to be logical and consistent he will have to make a similar change when he comes to subsection (e), which is part of the same section, and such a change is certain to occasion some discussion. If he does not make it there will be discussion just the same because of the *amendment he is now proposing. In order to make clear the significance of what is *being done, and which I think should not be done, let me state the purpose of the original sections.
The existing sections are to provide a method by which an application for a board of conciliation and investigation is to be made. There are two kinds of situations to be taken into account. One is where an application is to be made by a union, or by men who are members of a union, and the other is where the application comes from those who are not members of a union. The law as it exists requires that before an application can be made to the Government for the appointment of a board of conciliation and investigation where it affects union members there shall be a majority vote of those who are members of the union. That is to say that if a meeting of

the union is being held and if members wish to make application for a board a vote of the members present will have to be taken so that there will be something of record to show that the matter has been considered and that there was an actual majority in favour of making the application. There is a further provision as regards special meetings, that a notice shall be posted stating the object for which the meeting is called and that a ballot shall be taken at the meeting in reference to the particular subject in dispute. The minister is doing away with any necessity of calling any special meeting of the union to consider the matter, and is proposing to do away altogether with the necessity of taking any vote, with the result that if an application is made to the department a dispute may arise on the question as to whether a majority of those who belong to the union really made an application. Some employer might take exception to a hoard being granted on the ground that the majority required by the Act did not vote in favour of the application. There is, under the amendment proposed, no means of deciding that fact other than by taking the word of the particular persons who put in the application. As the Act stands to-day there is a recorded vote to which reference can be made and which is all sufficient to satisfy the minister as to the application having been made in the Tight way.
Now we come to the application to be made by any group of men who are not members of a trade union in regard to a dispute that arises. The Act at present requires that three days' notice shall be posted and that a vote shall he taken of the men who attend a meeting to discuss the question of an application to the Government for a board of conciliation and investigation. All parties know about it, those that are interested attend. If the majority decide in favour of an application for a board, they have a right to obtain a board in that way; a record of the vote on the application has been made, and it is beyond dispute. This has worked out, as far as 1 know, perfectly satisfactorily. It has occasioned trouble or embarrassment to no one. The minister now proposes to do away with that precaution and to say that there shall be no vote taken, he proposes to do away with the necessity of posting a three days' notice in regard to the calling of a meeting and simply to permit any group of men, without a vote and without a meeting, without any reference to any special matter in dispute, to make application to the Government for a board.
I think the effect of it will be to create all kinds of difficulties foT the minister in granting, or in determining whether he has the right or not to grant, a board, and I think it will, in many cases, act prejudicially to the interests of all concerned. I also 'think that it may lead to an undue interference with an established business by enabling any two men where it suits particular individuals, to go around with a sheet of paper and solicit the names of different men who may or may not belong to a union, and, obtaining the required number of names, .to secure from the Government the right to have the whole machinery of the Act set in motion.
In this connection I must point out the bearing of another amendment which the minister has .suggested-which I think is entirely wrong. Under the llaw as it. stood, witness fees were based on the rates allowed in the different provinces. But the minister has changed that provision so as to allow the payment of a minimum of $4 a day to witnesses, although when the Minister of Labour introduced the measure in the other House he asked that the minimum should be only $2 a day. Some discussion took place there as to the $2 not being a sufficient amount for experts, and the figure was changed to $4 so. as to arrive a't an all round figure which may apply to all .classes Of witnesses. The effect of bringing in this .amendment .along with the .permission to. allow payment of $4 to all witnesses will be .simply this: In regard to a large number of disputes that will be dealt with under this law, any two individuals in a mining camp, or anywhere else, who think that they would like to start an investigation into a business of a particular concern will go around among the members of a camp, tell them that if they so wish they will be called as witnesses in regard to a particular investigation and that they will get $4 a day as witnesses; and if these two persons get a majority, without any vote, without any meeting, without any discussion on the question one way or the other,-if the law is carried out, the Government will have to grant a board for such investigation. Now opening the door to possible proceedings of that kind is mischievous. It will only help, I think, ,in .some quarters to bring the Act into question in a way it has not been brought into question in the past. I would therefore like to make this last appeal to the minister-before he changes a section of the law which has not, so far as I am aware been embarrassing to any of the parties con-

cerned-that he leave well enough alone and not make these unnecessary amendments.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The leader of the Opposition should remember that the author of this Bill is not myself but the Minister of Labour who administers the Act. The committee, of course, is well aware of that. The leader of the Opposition has before argued the point that he now re-introduces. It is a fact that the Minister of Labour contemplates by this amendment that a board may >be requested- in any single case (1) either by the calling of a meeting and the securing of a majority of all the members affected at that meeting, or (2) by securing a majority without calling a meeting, and saying to the minister that such majority duly authorizing two of the officers to ask for the board has been secured. The minister is of opinion that if over one-half want the board, that should be sufficient evidence to him of the desire of the men at least. Though that half may not have voted at a meeting, if they make the request by petition he thinks that should be sufficient and he thinks it is a much better safeguard against abuse-the requirement of the majority imperatively in every case-than was the provision of the old law that in many cases enabled a very small minority to act simply because that small minority happened to be the majority present at a meeting. That is his opinion, and I must say it does seem most reasonable. I do not for a moment think the leader of the Opposition has anything but the good of the Act in view, but he will recognize that what he suggests would be a restriction on the men. If time shows that that restriction is requisite the Minister of Labour may come back with an amendment to that end; but I would be very much surprised if time should show it to be requisite. Now that is the sum and substance of the whole matter. To repeat in one sentence: The minister is of the opinion, and I commend his view to the committee, that a majority of the men should have the right to ask a. board if that majority is certain, though not evidenced by a vote at a meeting duly called. So long as there is a majority he does not want to restrict the right; but there must be a majority as distinct from the old prerequisite which required nothing more than a majority present at a meeting though that might not be more than 10 per cent of the men affected.
The Minister of Labour intends by the amendment of clause 4, which has already
[Mr. Mackenzie King'd
been passed, that $4 should be the minimum for an allowance to- witnesses inclusive of expenses, believing that all witnesses should get the same throughout Canada. I would not apprehend that men should be anxious for a board in order that they might substitute $4, inclusive of expenses, for the wages they were drawing. It would seem to me that they would be paying quite a heavy penalty for the board if that were their only object ini asking for it.

I am sorry I was not present when these amendments were before the committee a few days ago, but I desire to say a word or two with respect to them even at this late stage.
I think that the provision in subsection D of section 16 is entirely too loose. It reads:
by employees who are members of a trade union, by two of its officers duly authorized by a majority of the members of the union.
What does the word "duly" mean? It will cause any amount of dispute and confusion to arise. I would suggest that the word " duly " be stricken out entirely and that the paragraph should read:
"By two of its officers authorized in writing."
It would be well to have the authority given in writing otherwise you will find a man saying: "You told me on the street -corner to do so and so " and the response being made " No, I never told you anything of the sort." Whereas if the request received from the man on the street corner were signed by him it would be much better. As I see it the provision in its present form is useless.
Then take the provision that there shall be a minimum sum of $4 allowed for witness fees. The provision should not be in that form because a " minimum " of $4 means that the payments may be a great deal more than that amount. I have no objection whatever to the provision going through if the word " minimum " is stricken out. If the provision is left in its present form you will have people in one province claiming that they ought to get $6 or $8 a day because the Act only mentions a minimum. If the sum is fixed at $4 without any reference to minimum I have no objection to it. Then the witness will get $4 whether it is in the province of Prince Edward Island or the province of British Columbia. Leave the provision as it is -and it will result in all sorts of disputes because I know the kind of claims

that are put forth for witness fees and allowances of that kind.

I share the views which have been expressed by the ex-Minister of Labour (Mr. Crothers) I think the $4 well represents what may be due a witness for spending his day in the interest of social justice, and no encouragement to demands for a greater amount should be given by allowing the word " minimum " to remain. On the other hand, I agree with my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) that in these days of labour unrest no encouragement should he given to agitators or ill-advised persons who by their simple whim might direct a strike to take place unless a board is granted. I think that evidence of the desire of the men to have a board appointed should be very clearly demonstrated, not by mere word of mouth but in writing, as my hon. friend the ex-minister says-at all events it should be a document authenticated by the signatures of responsible people holding an official position in the union or in the local organization of the employees.
We must not do anything to bring this legislation into contempt. Let me say to my hon. friend who is now piloting the Bill through the House (Mr. Meighenj that this legislation-the credit for the drafting of which, 1 need not say, must he given to my hon. friend, the leader of the Opposition-enjoys to-day a world reputation. As my hon. friend knows, it has been adopted by several states of the Union, by some of the British dominions, and now there is before the French Parliament legislation based on our Industrial Disputes Act. Before I left France a few months ago it was my pleasure and my pride to hand over to the President of the Council, M. Millerand, all data, statistics and literature on what is generally called the Lemieux Act. He was preparing legislation for compulsory 'investigation and arbitration in ceitain cases of industrial disputes, and he repeated to me what he had said on previous occasions, that he knew of no better legislation to settle industrial troubles than the Canadian legislation. I would ask my hon. friend who is piloting the amendments to this legislation through the House to be very careful not to "denature" the spirit of this legislation-not tc so amend it as to bring it into contempt by the people. Therefore I would ask him not to press the amendment which he has just moved whereby some employees might
at any given moment by a mere whim ask for a board when no board was really needed. The desirability of putting the machinery of the Act into motion is always a very delicate question for the Minister of Labour to decide, and it must be known throughout the land that the machinery is put into motion only on a real stated case when there is autenticated evidence that a grievance exists and that a board is needed.

It
seems to me that there is a misapprehension in the minds of both the hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) with regard to the intent of the amendments of this Act. The original clause provides:
If made by employees members of a trade union shall be signed by two of its officers duly authorized by a majority vote of the members of the union, or by a.vote taken by ballot of the members of the union present at a meeting called on not less than three days' notice for the purpose of discussing the question.
The amendment provides:
That if by its employees members of a union authority shall be by a majority vote of all the members of that particular union, and not by a majority at any particular meeting.
That is, the majority of the members present at any particular meeting as provided for in the original clause. So that instead of making it easier, the amendment is simply providing that the request shall represent the desire of a majority of the members of the union affected, employing the words introduced by the minister on the suggestion of the hon. member for Tim-iskaming (Mr. McDonald).
With regard to the second objection raised by the hon. leader of the Opposition, I am not going to be dogmatic in regard to it, but I think if you read clause (e) you will find that provision is clearly made for calling a meeting on three days' notice and taking a vote where the men affected are not members of a union.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Is that my hon. friend's impression of the amendment?
I would say so.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: If my hon. friend will read the amendment he will find he is quite mistaken.

The amendment reads:
By employees some or all of whom are not members of a trade union, by two of their

number duly uthorized by a majority of such employees. If such authorization is obtained in whole or in part by a vote at a meeting, such meeting shall be called on not less than three days' notice and the vote shall be by ballot.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The amendment now means that it by any chance they should take a vote and decide to make application they cannot take a vote unless there has been three days' notice of the meeting given. The old law said that there must be three days' notice given, and then a vote at the meeting "would decide whether or not an application would be made. The amendment is quite different and changes the whole effect of the clause. As it is now the amendment proposed leaves it open to any two men to go around in any camp or community that is unorganized, get a certain number of names, and thereby compel ilhe granting of a board. I am sure tbait my hon. friend the present Minister of Labour (Hon.- Mir. Robertson) and his predecessor (Mr. Orothers-) will agree with me that that is not a wise change in the Act. I believe that the intent of the Minister of Labour is thoroughly good, bult as given expression to in these amendments it is thoroughly bad, and I hope that the amendments will not be persisted in.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I should make reference to the new suggestion 'that has been made and which has been supplemented by the remarks of the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux). I would feel like taking the responsibility of accepting an amendment, moving it myself for that matter, to make it clearer that the authorization must be in writing, because I feel that that is the intention of the minister, following the expression used as the Rill was submitted to this House. If that is done in clause (d), it would require also to be done in clause (e); so I move:
-to further amend clause 2 by striking out the word "duly" where it appears in the twenty-third and twenty-ninth lines of the first page of the Bill and by adding after the word "authorized" where it appears in both of the said lines, the words "in writing."
The remarks I made before, of course, apply to the request of the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux). It is one of the infirmities under which our system suffers that in one House the minister responsible, and who has the actual administration, cannot be present. That is inevitable, either in the House or in the Senate, and it happens now that we suffer under that in the House of Commons The minister in charge of this Bill undoubtedly believes in the Act and in the prin-

ciple underlying it. He has had to do with the administration of the Act for many years in his capacity as member and officer of the trade union, and for some considerable time in his capacity as Minister of Labour. He thinks the Act is to be improved by enabling a majority to express itself in any way. It is conceivable, of course, that the provisions o.f the Act may be abused even now, but he is removing one source of abuse, the case where a mere minority may put the whole Act into operation,-because even if three days' notice is given, members of a trade union may find it difficult to attend a meeting. He is removing that, and having removed it he does not feel like going further and hampering further the employees. He thinks that if it is difficult to hold a meeting the men ought to be allowed to express themselves by petition in writing. That being his deliberate view, and that view being not open, in my humble judgment,-which, I admit, is not worth very much-to serious objection, I do not feel like taking the responsibility of going further in the way of amendment to the clause.
Mr. CROTHERiS:	The amendment proposed by the minister does not sufficiently safeguard the interests of all parties concerned. I am inclined to the belief that the workingmen ought to have an opportunity of discussing matters of so much importance. If this amendment carries, any individual can go round and get Tom, Dick and Harry to sign this paiper asking for a board. On the other hand, if the men gathered together in a meeting they would have full opportunity of discussing the situation, pro and con, and it might be found that few were in favour of asking for a board. I believe that the interests of the workingmen, the employer and the public will be best served if the men have an opportunity of discussing the matter before a board is asked for. Much difficulty may be created if the principle of the amendment is adopted.

I quite agree with my hon. friend (Mr. Crothers). Hon. members on bolth sides should regard favourably the presentation off any just grievance by the workingmen. But on the other hand, we must not allow the workingmen to be worked by some ingenious agitator who may easily go from one mine to another, from one establishment to another, and endeavour to create trouble between capital and labour. I want to give this legislation a proper working basis and to see that when put into motion the machinery of

the law shall not ibe hampered. But let us not forget thiaJt there are in all countries people who are attempting to create- the word may seem to he a little strong- revolution. The workingmen are amply protected toy this legislation; -my hon. friend should, not insist upon affording a weapon which agitators may use to bring the legislation into contempt. Has there been any petition from any labour organization asking foT this amendment?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I ooulld not say as to that, but I stated when the Bill was here before that the amendment in its present form was (approved by the Trades and Labour Congress through its executive. That is my information from (the Minister of Labour.

I travelled lately with Mr. Tom Moore, and we discussed (this legislation. He did not suggest any such amendment as this, but he did suggest, as the leader of the (Opposition did when' the matter was previously discussed, that a provision making the legislation applicable to oonstatoles should be inserted in the Act. I would like to have the views of Mr. Moore with regard to this proposed amendment, because he is a level-headed labour man; he is not an agitator.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
For many
years the Dominion Trades and Labour Congress, through their executive, have waited on the Government once a year. I have looked at the proceedings as reported and I have found nothing in any representations which they have made through the executive at that meeting which pertains at all to the changes now proposed. I am perfectly sure that such representations have not been made as coming from any discussions or resolutions of the Dominion Trades and Labour Congress, What I think has probably happened is that, as regards paragraph (d) one or two members of the executive have expressed to the minister the opinion that where there is a trade union, they would prefer to leave to the trade union leaders the matter of getting a majority of the union to ask for a board instead of having a meeting. I can understand their wishes in that matter. The minister, however, has gone further than that; he has added paragraph (e) to some extent paralleling paragraph (d). Paragraph (e) deals with men who are not organized at all or some of whom are organized, and in seeking to meet the wishes of others in regard to paragraph (d) he has got into a difficulty, he never foresaw as regards paragraph (e). According to the Bill as it stands now, any two men can go around and secure (signatures, and even if the minister puts in the amendment of the hon. member for Elgin West (Mr. Crothers), that is, to add the words " in writing," that will not alter matters for they will get the signatures in writing. Therefore, notwithstanding what the motives of those two men may be, the Government will be compelled to grant a board and to allow the company's business to be examined by the different representatives who would be put on that board. If the door is left open in that way, opportunity is going to he given for all kinds of mischievous proceedings, and inas-



much as this paragraph is the one that relates simply to proceedings asking for a board, the minister would be well advised to leave this section alone for the present.
If the Dominion Trades and Labour Congress, through their executive, ask for this change at a subsequent session, we shall then be justified in considering the matter further. But in the absence of any representations in writing which the minister can present to Parliament, I do not think that simply for the sake of forcing this through, he ought to go contrary to what I believe would be the wish of the Minister of Labour himself if he were in a position to be in this House and to see the effect of the amendment as it is pointed out at the present time.
Mr. ME1GHEN:	The minister has read
the arguments presented by the hon. member including the ones hearing on this very point.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I laid them before the minister separately at the time, and he told me that this Bill had been laid before the executive of the Congress and had been approved. I did not say that the Congress had, either in writing or in any other way, requested this change, and I do not know whether they did or not. I merely know that it is the opinion of the minister-and as to its correctness I have not the faintest doubt in the world-that this change has been approved by the Congress.
There is something to which the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) referred to which I did not refer. I think if my memory serves me right, the Bill as introduced provided a uniform allowance of $4 a day, but objection was raised in the other House-we are all abandoning the rule now, so I shall have to follow suit- that there would be no provision at all for two cases. I am not sufe whether the two cases were mentioned, but one was, and the one that was mentioned was that there was no provision that would enable the board to rely upon the attendance of expert witnesses. Consequently, a minimum was fixed. The other case is this.
5 p.m. Very often boards are held at points where it is impossible that $4 will be sufficient to cover anything like remuneration and expense, or even expenses alone. Usually, this fee will do so, and the minister feels that $4 will be virtually the uniform chbrge everywhere, but he submitted to the argument that it would not cover every case and consequently, he

yielded the point and had the fee of $4~ fixed as the minimum.
In Ontario, I understand expert witnesses are paid a very much larger fee than the ordinary witness fee.

Section 34 of the Act
reads:
Every person who is summoned and duly attends as a witness shall be entitled to an allowance for expenses according to the scale for the time being in force with respect to witnesses in civil suits in the superior courts in the province where the inquiry is being conducted.
I understand now that we fix the amount of the witness fee at $4.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: As a'minimum.
My hon. friend says that this word " minimum " is to protect the case of an expert.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is what was urged in the Senate.

It is not necessary. In the Quebec courts an expert is entitled to a larger fee than an ordinary witness receives. Of course, it has to be established that he is an expert. In my own practice I have seen quite often-and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) knows it too- that such expert witnesses as architects, doctors or civil engineers appearing before a court are entitled by the laws of the province to a special fee. Therefore, my hon. friend is opening a dangerous ground for fees which, under ordinary circumstances, might be quite satisfactory at the fixed sum of $4.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It was the minister's intention to fix the fee at $4.
Why say "minimum"?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I must admit I do not see much force in the objection to which I referred and which was raised in the Senate. It would seem to me the objection was covered, but it is easy to conceive of cases where, for example, if the inquiry were held, say in Ottawa and men were brought here, it would take $4 a day to pay their expenses; they would be getting less than they were getting before. This is an allowance to cover expenses and fees. The section does not refer to Lees at all. It reads:
Every person who is summoned and duly attends as a witness shall be entitled to an allowance tor expenses according to the scale for the time being in force-
"With respect to witnesses in civil suits."

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, the allowance is to witnesses in civil suits; it is an allowance for expenses. As I understand it, the whole allowance they will get now is $4.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: A minimum of $4.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is what I mean. But the minimum of $4 is to cover everything the witness gets, because everything he gets is an expense allowance. That is what I am arguing.
A man's transportation is over and above the amount he gets per day?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, he gets transportation,

The Minister of Justice knows that after a case is finished, the witnesses will go before a registrar of the court or the prothonotary and have their fees taxed. Those fees include their travelling allowance and expenses for being called as witnesses in the case. If they stay one day, two days, three days, a week they are paid so much per day in addition to their travelling expenses.

The question raised by this section involves an addition to the rights and powers of the workman, making it easier for him to obtain a board under the Act, and in that sense, I think the change is to be commended. There may be, although such have not been clearly pointed out within my hearing, special cases where it is difficult to obtain a meeting, but I would understand that in 99 cases out of 100, a meeting of the men belonging to a union could easily be convened because they will more or less live in the same neighbourhood. As regards the form of the section, I think it is rather left-handedly drawn, and I would suggest that it would he much clearer, no matter what principle is to he adopted if it read in this way:
The application and the declaration accompanying it shall be signed, if made, by two officers of any trade union so appearing who have been authorised in writing by a majority of the members thereof.
At present it reads:
The application and the declaration accompanying it shall be signed, if made by employees who are members of a trade union, by two of its officers duly authorised by a majority of the members of the union.
I do not like that word " duly." I agree with my hon. friend from West Elgin (Mr. Crothers) and my hon. friend from Maison-neuve (Mr. Lemieux) that it does not leave the form of authorization sufficiently clear in the public mind. One union might consider that it was duly authorized by one course of procedure, while another union might adopt an altogether different course, also under the conviction that it was duly authorized. The authorization should be clear and beyond dispute. I think that the section as it is proposed is undoubtedly adding to rather than taking from the powers of workmen to obtain boards, and in that respect it should be commended.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I think that the explanation of the difficulties, we are having at the moment arises from the fact that while there are two clauses which we have been discussing, some of us have had our minds fixed only on subsection (d) while others have been speaking in reference to subsection (e). The minister just a moment ago said that he had acquainted the Minister of Labour with what I had said and that that hon. gentleman was quite aware of the points I had raised. May I mention the fact that up to to-day I have not discussed subsection (e) at all. The point I am raising in regard to subsection (e) I was reserving until we had reached that subsection, and in discussing subsection (d) I pointed out at the time these objections: first of all, of departing from the requirement that a vote be taken and registered in a record, and secondly, that some notice of the meeting be made compulsory so that those interested should be present. These sections were in the previous Act in the provisions corresponding with subsection (d) of this Act, and it would have been well to retain them in that subsection. However, they have been stricken out; and while I can quite understand that officers of unions may have made representations to the minister that they preferred to have subsection (d) in the form in which he now proposes it, I will venture the opinion that no representative of any union ever asked the minister to change subsection (e) to the form in which it now stands, and I am perfectly sure the Minister of Labour does not yet perceive the full significance of this subsection as it now stands or he would not permit it to come before this committee. May I suggest to my hon. friend from North Perth (Mr. Morphy) a concrete case and leave it to his own judgment as to whether he thinks it wise that the change proposed

should be made? Let us assume that the (Street railway system of Stratford is operated by men, none of whom are members of a trade union. The men that work on that railway may or may not be organized,
I am not sure; but I am assuming for the sake of argument that none of them are members of a trade union. Under the amendment now being introduced, any person who has a grievance against the railway .system of Stratford can go to any two men employed on that railway and persuade them to circulate a petition among their fellow-workers asking for a board of investigation into the operations of that railway system. They may say:	"There
are certain things which we desire to bring out in regard to this company s business, and we can bring them out if we obtain a board, because we can put on that board any person we please and so bring the company into court, so to speak. They can investigate the books of the company, compel the production of documents, examine witnesses under oath, and drag the business of that transportation system into a court of investigation and have its affairs inquired into at the expense of the Government, all at the instance of any two men -who, for any consideration that may be offered them, can contrive to secure enough names to a petition asking for a board. Would my hon. friend from North Perth wish to have the great public utilities of this country-the street railways, the railway systems of Canada, the coal mines, the metaliiferous mines, the telegraphs, the telephones, and all other great public service utilities-would my hon. friend, I say, desire to have these large and important enterprises subjected to interference of that kind on the part of people who may happen to he nothing but mischief makers? If he would not, he cannot support the amendment, which reads:
by two of their number duly authorized by a majority of such employees.
The old Act required that there should be a majority vote, and further, that there should be a notice of three days so that every one likely to be affected could attend the meeting and say whether or not the application should be put in. I am as sure as that I am standing here that the Minister of Labour would not for one moment bring in the amendment if he saw its significance. I am sure he has not seen it, and I therefore again ask my hon. friend not to press it at this time.

The
leader of the Opposition apparently desires 
what I was asking for when the Bill was before the House a few evenings ago, and that is, that before a board shall be asked for there shall have been an expression of opinion by a very substantial number of those who were interested and not at the instance of two or three sore heads, if I may use that expression. Under the law as is has hitherto stood, all that was necessary was for two agitators to arrange to call a (meeting by giving three days' notice. There might be half a dozen men or so at the meeting, Which might be called at such time and in such manner as might not meet the convenience of the employees generally. But if a majority of the men present 'at that meeting voted in favour of the application then they had the right to demand a board. Under the amendment as it has been introduced there must be a majority of all the imen. Now, the assumption of my hon. friend that agitators can go arourjd and get a written authorization asking for a board simply at the request of some who might desire to embarrass the company for which they were working, must be based on the previous assumption that the men, to say the very least, have very little sense of responsibility in regard to their work or in regard to what they owe the public; and if that is the case, surely it is a safeguard to provide that the board shall be granted only at the .demand of a majority of all the men and not because a very limited minority, as would undoubtedly happen in many instances, might ask for it. Under the Act as it stands at pr sent all that is required is that there shall be 'a majority of those present. I am not betraying any confidence when I say that I have discussed this subject personally with members of trades unions and also with the Minister of Labour, and I think that this provision is a wise one, It provides that there shall be a responsible body of employees behind any application for a Board of Conciliation. As stated by my hon. (friend from Maisonneuve, there are agitators throughout the length and breadth of this country who are ready to take advantage of any opportunity which may be inadvertently afforded them to create disturbance. It would be unwise to leave the door open for them to call meetings recklessly :

And take a surprise
vote:
Mr. NICHOLSON fAlgoma):	Yes. Yet,
if it were possible for a small number of men to convene a meeting and call for a

board, just such conditions as are apprehended might be brought about.
-Mr. MEIGHEN:	I think the committee
will readily concede that I have not tried to push this Bill unduly either in the House or in Committee. This is the third period to which it has been postponed, and if I had any doubt as to the Minister of Labour properly apprehending the clause I would ask that the committee rise again. But I have no doubt in the matter, because I know that the minister understands that he is here giving power to a majority to express itself by petition without a meeting, as well as power to a majority to express itself by petition at a meeting. He is giving that power to the majority whether they are all members of a trade union and likewise giving it to a majority whether they are not all members of a trade union but he feele that he can rely on the sense of responsibility of the majority, and, insisting on the majority, he does not feel like adding any other restrictions.

We are experiencing
this afternoon one of the inconveniences of our constitution or of the rules of the House. Ingenious, able, persuasive and eloquent as my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior is, yet everybody feels that there is a strong doubt running through his mind as to whether this amendment is a wise one. He himself expresses quite cautiously, of course, regret that the minister in charge of the Department of Labour, one of the most important, if not the most important, during the present crisis, is not allowed to come and explain his legislation before this House as he has explained it before the other House. My hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) is about to present amendments to the British North America Act. Has not the time come for some amendment which will enable ministers of the Crown to appear in each Chamber as their presence is needed according to the requirements of the legislation promoted in Parliament? We have an example this afternoon, because we must all realize that, notwithstanding the great ability of my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior, it would be a great advantage if the Minister of Labour were allowed to come on the floor of this House and explain why this amendment is proposed. We have an illustration this afternoon of the illogical position in which ministers are placed. In a few days legislation will be brought into this House which would require under ordinary circumstances the presence of the Postmaster 'General. The Postmaster General is asking Parliament to increase his Tight of taxing the people of Canada. He will not be on the floor of this House to explain his legislation. Why not have here what they have in other countries-responsible ministers passing from one Chamber to another and explaining their legislation? There is nothing contrary to common sense in that, it is pure logic, and as the British constitution is the result of precedent coming slowly down from one generation to another, why not in this House, (where progress is the banner word upon every one's lips, amend the constitution so as to permit a minister of the Crown to appear in each Chamber? Perhaps the Minister of Labour would be able to convince us that this amendment is wise, but apparently it is not a wise amendment since we find objection to it on both sides of the House.

speakerposition: stagedirection

speechtext: Does the Government contemplate making any new appointments?
