speechtext: This Bill does not involve any new appointments for the present. The court now consists of the judge who .will be the president and an assistant judge, and the latter will naturally be the new puisne judge.

I certainly favour the change making the assistant judge a puisne judge, especially in view of the fact that he is so efficient a judge and possesses the confidence of all litigants in the country. I do not know why an exception is made in regard to the power to make general rules. Why should this power be confined to the president of the court? The rules of any other court are generally adopted by the judges of that court, the puisne judges acting in common with the president.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That is the law as it stands at the present time. But here, I
might point out, you have a court composed of two judges, and supposing those two judges did not agree on a particular rule, it would not be possible to make that rule. I think that is a sufficient reason why we should designate the president.
I think it would be more regular to call the president the "chief justice," following the practice in our Superior Courts.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Parliament at the
session of 1919 decided that question, when some understanding was come to in regard to it with the members of the court: While there may be some advantages in uniformity, still I do not know that any evil is done by using this designation, "President of the Exchequer Court," and it being already on the statute book I did not see any sufficient reason to change it.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 2-Power to appoint a deputy judge.
This is rather an extraordinary section. I would like the minister to explain it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Under section 140 of the Exchequer Court Act any person may be appointed a judge of the court who is or has been judge of a superior court or of a county court or who is a barrister of ten years' standing at the bar of any of the provinces. This section merely refers to those qualifications.
Is it not an innovation to appoint a judge temporarily?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: To make such an appointment would be an innovation; but to .make a provision for deputy judges is not at all an innovation. For instance, there ,is provision in our law foir the appointment of deputy judges in the county court under similar circumstances; and under the law as i't stands there is provision for ,the 'appointment of a deputy judge for the Exchequer Court. That provision required modification because there was only one judge and-

I quite understand that there are temporary appointments, but what I want to direct the attention of the minister to is that under this amendment a temporary judge appointed at the pleasure of the Governor in Council might be appointed to try one particular case. I think that is objectionable, and that it would be better legislation to select a temporary judge from members of the bench.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There is perhaps ground for objection on that account. This particular wording has been adopted because in the past it was found that if you appoint a deputy judge to act during the absence or illness of a judge, you have no definite thing that settles the moment when such absence or illness ceases. Therefore it was thought that the Governor in Council might be trusted to terminate the office of a deputy judge when the purpose of his appointment has been served. However, I would have no objection to make that read:
or upon a certificate of the President of the Court that the purpose to be served had been accomplished.

or something like that, so that we would have an official declaration of when the powers terminated1. Before making that amendment, however, there is another amendment which occurs to me, and which I think will commend itself to the committee. It seems to me that perhaps it is objectionable that the Governor in Council should have, as under the present terms of the section, general power to appoint a deputy judge for any reason, which he deems sufficient. I think there should be some check on that power. Therefore I desire to move that the section be amended by inserting in line twenty-two between the words "or" and "for" the words "at the request of the President." The section would then read:
The Governor in Council may, in the. case of the sickness or absence from Canada or engagement upon other duty of the President or the Puisne Judge, or, at the request of the President, for any other reason which he deems sufficient,-
and so on. The effect of that will be to limit the power of the Governor in Council to the three specified cases: Sickness, absence from Canada, or engagement upon other duties, of the president or of the puisne judge. I would be quite happy, however, if the hon. gentleman can suggest the language, to meet the objection which has been made.
Is this not new legislation? I cannot recall a case where power has been vested in a judge to ask for the appointment, or practically to make the appointment, of a deputy judge.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
He will not appoint the .deputy judge; he will simply request an .appointment. If the President of the Court exposes the necessity for there being a deputy judge, then the Governor in Council is empowered to appoint one, but the Presi-

dent of the Court does not designate the man who shall be appointed, nor is the Governor in Council bound to make the appointment. There is analagous power in the case of the Superior Courts of the province of Quebec and the Court of Appeal. If the Chief Justice of the Court of Appeal represents that by reason of illness or some other impediment preventing one of the judges from carrying out his duties there is occasion for such an appointment!' there is power to appoint an assistant judge. So with the Superior Court, and my impression is, with other provincial courts. Quite recently we made a Similar provision for the purpose of providing an acting judge in the Supreme Court in cases where there might be occasion for doing so. This power to appoint a deputy judge has always existed in regard to the Exchequer Court. The difference is that we have to provide not merely for cases of absence or illness o<f the president or of the puisne judge, but also for absence through other causes which we cannot at the moment specify. For instance, the parties interested might be close relatives of the president of the court or of the puisne judge; there are many cases where a judge might find himself disqualified. These general terms were adopted to avoid the necessity for foreseeing all these cases. At the same time we are putting such a check upon the exercise of the power that there need be no apprehension that it will be unduly exercised. It cannot be exercised unless the President of the Court asks for it, and if the reasons given are deemed insufficient there is no obligation on the Governor in Council to exercise it.

I do not object to the authority being in the Governor in Council to appoint an assistant or deputy judge for the time being and for special cause. If the minister will provide that the selection shall be made from among the judges of the Superior Court in the province where the action arises, I shall have no objection.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It is not proposed that the selection should be limited to judges oi the Superior Court, because if you did that you might be taking away from his own work a man who could not very well be spared. The qualifications required in the man to be appointed are exactly the same as will be required of a man to be appointed as judge, that is, he should be a judge of a Superior or County court, or a barrister of ten years' standing in the province. I do not think that the deputy judge should be required to possess greater qualifications than the judge himself.

Mr. McKENZIE .[DOT] A barrister of ten years' standing does not become a competent judge all at once. We have seven Supreme Court judges in Nova Scotia,-and I do not think that any occasion would arise to prevent any one of them from stepping outside his usual work to try a special case. I assume that conditions in other provinces are the same. There should be some provision to secure for the purposes of this- provision an experienced man who is in the public eye and against whose appointment there could be no reasonable objection.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
This is only to provide
for possible cases, which will be very few and far between. If one of these judges dies, the public will have to accept a barrister of ten years' standing as the permanent judge. Is there any very great danger that that barrister of ten years' standing would not be competent to act as deputy judge? The qualifications sufficient to justify a man's selection as permanent head of the court ought to be sufficient to justify his employment as deputy judge. Under this Bill, you may appoint as deputy judge a judge of another court if he be available, but to make it essential that you should take him away creates a situation where you may be embarrassed because there are courts and judges who have all the work they can do,

As these extraordinary
powers are being asked for probably on account of increased business before that tribunal, instead of appointing a temporary judge, why not have a third judge appointed permanently?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That has been considered, and we have given to the registrar certain powers contained in a subsequent section of this Bill, thus providing ample man-power, if I may use that expression, to carry on all the work of the court so long as that man-power is available. But it is to be foreseen that you may have accidents when your actual men are not all available, and this is merely to provide that when that accident happens-, we shall be able to call somebody in to do the work. The hon. gentleman's remedy would be to provide more men than are necessary to do the work, as a rule, because occassionally you may require, not an additional judge, but just somebody to take the place of a man who drops out on account of illness or some other cause of that kind. We have, as I have said, .satisfied ourselves
with conferring on the registrar the powers contained in a subsequent section, so that we shall have quite sufficient to attend to this work, with the presiding and the puisne judges as long as they are both available. But in the uncertainty of human events, we have to provide for the accidental cases where one of them might not be available, and we take the means of providing a temporary person instead of loading the country with a permanent judge at a permanent salary so as to have somebody, perhaps, for one week in the year, when he may be required to take the place of a judge who is ill.

What salary will you
give to this temporary judge?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No provision is made
in this Bill for a special salary to this deputy judge, because we cannot tell for how long we may want him. We may want him only for a week. We shall not give him a permanent salary because he will not be a permanent judge; he will be appointed when occasion requires, and his powers will terminate when the occasion for them terminates and just as is done with deputy judges provided for in the county courts, no provision is made for a salary. In most instances deputy judges who have been appointed in connection with county courts have worked without salary. In some exceptional eases where a long period of time is- involved or some exceptional heavy work has been put upon them, power has been asked to provide for remuneration for this temporary work. This is not a permanent position in any sense of the .word at all; it is making provision for a possible occasional, temporary need.

This power conferred
on the 'Governor in Council by this clause may not be used very frequently, but it creates a precedent. I think it is the first time. we give the Governor in Council power to appoint temporary judges.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The power already exists with regard to the Exchequer Court.

What is the change
then?
Mr. DOlHERTY: The change as I pointed out is that in the present legislation, we .are not limiting the power to specified cases of necessity.

speechtext: The House resumed from May 6, consideration in committee of Bill No. 12 (Hon. Mr. Guthrie) respecting the election of members of the House of Commons and the electoral franchise-Mr. Boivin in the Chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
When progress was
last reported upon this Bill, all of the clauses and schedules had been read and considered. Paragraph (k) of clause 2; clauses 29, 32, 37, 44, 45, 63 and 101; the amendmets proposed by the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Turgeon) to clause 37 and by the hon. the Acting Solicitor General (Mr. Guthrie) to clauses 29, 44 and 101, were allowed to stand for further consideration. Clauses 19 and 76, which provide for the expenditure of money, cannot be adopted until the House has concurred in the required resolution. The other clauses have been adopted. Clause 29 is under consideration. Mr. Guthrie has moved to amend clause 29 by adding to subclause 2 the following words:
Provided that no disability imposed by paragraph (b) of subsection four of section eight of "The Naturalization Act," chapter thirty-eight of the statutes of 1919 (first session) shall disentitle a person on that ground alone to the said Certificate.
Mr. Euler has moved in amendment to the amendment to strike out in its entirely subclause 2 of clause 29 of the Bill. The question is on the sub-amendment.

When this committee 'rose the other evening I was dealing with the amendment ol the hon. member of South Waterloo (Mr. Euler) striking subolause 2 of section 29 out of the Act. The contention is that all the purpose of a franchise Act of a liberal and proper kind can be served by the enactment of the first paragraph of clause 29 and that the second paragraph is not necessary and is merely making it difficult for a certain class of people who are entitled to vote to

exercise the right of the franchise. The first part of section 29 reads as follows:
Save as in this Act otherwise provided, every person, male or female, shall be qualified to vote at the election of a member, who, not being: an Indian ordinarily resident on an Indian reservation,
(a)	is a British subject by birth or naturalization ; and,
(b)	is of the full age of twenty-one years; and,
(c)	has ordinarily resided in Canada for at least twelve months and in the electoral district wherein such person seeks to vote for at least two months immediately preceding the issue of the writ of election.
The contention is that all that is necessary to provide for the qualification of everyone is to stipulate that he is a Briish subject, is twenity-one years of age, has resided in Canada for twelve months and has resided in the district in, which he seeks to vote for two months. That has been the rule since Confederation. I was saying, the other evening when, we ended the day's debate, that, if that is not the intention of the Government and if they are determined to put this Act through, it should be made as easy as possible for applicants who must apply for the certificate provided for under subsection 2 of section 29 to get that certificate. As it is now, there is only one class of officials to whom applicants can -apply, that is judges of the Supreme and 'County Courts. I think that both these classes of judges are entitled to hear applications for naturalization under the present Naturalization Act. The subsection says that applications -shall be heard before the peqple who are authorized to 'hear applications under the Naturalization Act. I would also -point out that women, young men or old men, who may need these certificates, are just -as important and deserving a class -as men who were seeking to get away from -service under the Military .Service Act and that the same facilities for application should be given to these men and women who will seek these certificates that were given to men who were applying for exemption. Under the -law providing for exemption there were thirty courts in the three counties of Cape Breton, Richmond and Victoria. In that large district there is only one judge residing at -Sydney and if this Act goes through any person looking for a certificate and residing in the counties of Richmond, Cape Breton or Victoria must go to that one judge in order to make application. I submit this is an extraordinary measure as some will be .150 miles away fro-m this judge's office in the city of Sydney, and it is practically impossible for people at the
extreme ends of these districts, or for that matter in other parts of the districts, except in iSyndey, to apply for the certificate. I further said to the minister-and I wish to receive -some attention in connection with this matter-that there are not sufficient grounds given for the application. The specific grounds upon which one -applies for this certificate are not set out at all. On page 83 of the Bill itself there are certain classes of questions prescribed in connection with Form K 2, as follows:
Interrogatories to be administered orally, under oath or affirmation, to applicants in person for registration as voters.
The questions that shall be asked of the applicant are made perfectly clear. He will be asked:
1.	What is your surname?
2.	What is your full Christian name or names?
3.	Where is your ordinary place of residence and what is your post office address?
4.	What is your occupation?
5.	Do you now reside in polling division No.
	 (or as the case may be) of the electoral district of	 for which you now
apply to be registered?
6.	Are you of the full age of twenty-one years?
7.	Are you a British subject?
8.	Are you such by birth or by naturalization? State which.
9.	If by naturalization when and how were you naturalized?
10.	Have you a certificate from a judge entitling you to be registered as a voter?
These questions-there are some more- make it perfectly clear to the applicant for registration what- he has to answer, and if any person feels that he cannot answer them he need not go to the trouble of applying. I submit that when a person has to go a long distance, perhaps ISO or 200 miles, -to a judge for the certificate which will be required under subsection 2, he at least should have some conception of the questions that he would be required to answer when he comes before the judge. I presume that an application can be made on behalf of the applicant by a lawyer or some other person who is entitled to appear be fore the court. A lawyer preparing a case under subclause 2 of section 29 has very little intimation of the kind of material in -the shape of evidence that he will be expected to put 'before the judge. If this Bill must pass and this requirement is to be exacted from people before they can vote, the leas-t that can -be done is to give those people some idea of what they will have to answer. Under the Naturalization Act it is well laid down what the applicant has to do, what he has to know, what he must provide for; and if he cannot comply with

those requisites it will be absolutely unnecessary for him to apply.
On another occasion I pointed out the rights of the men and the women who will be disfranchised by section 2 unless they get a certificate. I think it was the minister himself who pointed out that these people never had the right, to vote, and consequently are not suffering any loss; that the granting of the franchise is a privilege that must, in some special way, be conferred upon an individual. I do not think that that argument is as strong as it might appear. Even if it were all right and worthy of its full face value, the Act of 1918 which conferred the right to' vote upon women in Canada explicitly gave them the franchise. I am only dealing with women who were British subjects on the 24th of May, 1918. The Act referred to gave votes to women in express terms; and if they are to be deprived-in an indirect way by the words of subsection 2 of section 29 of the Franchise Act-of the right to vote, we are depriving them of a right which they now hold and can exercise until this Bill goes into force. I need not tell the minister or this committee that the right to vote is a property right. It is regarded not only in this country, but in Great Britain and in other countries of equal civilization, absolutely as a property right, and interference with it is regarded as an interference with a property right. Thus if a man is deprived of his vote by any individual putting obstacles in his way he can go into the courts of the country and sue for damages. That is not anything new, it has been done over and over again, showing conclusively that the exercise of the right to the franchise is tangible absolute property, and ,the taking of it away from a man is taking away his property. I submit, therefore, that if the minister insists upon passing subclause 2 now before the committee, he will be passing a law that takes away from thousands of women in Canada a right which they now possess and which may be called their tangible and absolute property. Now let me deal with the other point, that unless the right to vote is conferred upon a British subject he does not possess it. The old Act says:
An Alien to whom a certificate of naturalization is granted shall, within Canada be entitled to all political and other rights, powers and privileges, and be subject to all obligations to which a natural born British subject is entitled.
I am sure that no person possessing ordinary common sense would for one

moment argue that does not imply the right to vote. Such a person has got to have all political and other rights, powers and privileges of a British subject born on British soil. Will any person say that a British subject, born on British soil, is not entitled to vote if he is otherwise qualified? I submit that he is so entitled and that this was the purpose of the old Naturalization Act, chapter 77 of the Revised Statutes. The present Act, which was passed after the war began, and after we were given every opportunity of fully considering its effects provides as follows:
A person to whom a certificate of Naturalization is granted by the Secretary of State of Canada shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, be entitled to all political and other rights, powers -and privileges, and be subject to all obligations, duties and liabilities, to which a natural-born British subject is entitled or subject, and as from the date of his naturalization have to all intents and purposes the status of a natural-born British subject.
That is the Act we passed in 1919, and that is the law to-day without any amendment or interference of any kind. I submit again that there i-s no question as to what is implied in the statement "entitled to all political and other rights, powers and- privileges;" it means of course that a man has the right to vote. Take the case of a Belgian woman * who before the war came to this country and married a Canadian. Under our law she became a British subject. Such a woman, let us say, has remained in this country, has made the Dominion heT own country, so- to speak. She has 'been standing by us and has continued on the most friendly terms; hut when we come to give the vote we say to that Belgian woman, a British subject and a citizen of this country: You cannot vote'; because of a disturbance in this country, when we. got into a bad humour, we are going to visit the sins and iniquities of another country upon you; and although you have for years been a British subject, although you have given birth to and brought up children in this country, although you have worshipped at the shrines where Canadian men and women worship, although you have fulfilled all the obligations of British citizenship and we have nothing to say against you- nevertheless when you come to the poll on election day we must refuse you the right to British citizenship. We ask hon. gentlemen opposite, why? I do not wish to use any strong language here, but I do not think there is a man living within the four corners of Canada who can give a satisfactory answer as to why a woman of that class should be deprived of the Tight of

exercising the franchise in common with her husband.
I have already pointed out that I would not have so much fault to find with the Government in this connection if they had limited themselves to the disabilities which they have enforced in paragraph (b) of subsection 4, of clause 8 of the Naturalization Act-chapter 38 of the statutes of last year- and deprived aliens from enemy countries of the right to become naturalized for ten years. There would at least be some consistency about such action; they would he meting out the same treatment to those people when it came to naturalization as in the case of the exercise -off the franchise. But we Ihave widened the application of the proposed law altogether and made it apply to everybody who crosses the Atlantic to Canada unless they come from a British country. A German woman who went to the United States some years ago, became an American citizen theTe, and then located in Canada, or a Turkish woman who became naturalized in the United States and then came to this country, would have a right t-o vote; but a refined woman who came from France, or other friendly country in Europe, and passed all the educational tests of the class to which she belongs, would have no such right. Even a coloured woman, as has already been pointed out, or some other woman of no refinement at all, belonging to Mexico or some country of Central America, who marries a man and comes to -Canada, has the right to the franchise. Mr. Chairman, I submit to you that we are here 'sowing the seeds of difficulties and differences which the youngest member of this Chamber will not live to see the end of.
Why, Sir, we are teaching foreigners to respect our flag-and that is a proper thing to do; we are teaching foreigners young and old to sing "God save the King"; we are telling them that they are entitled to all the rights and privileges which we possess. On our days of celebration, on the Queen's birthday and Dominion Day, we gather the children together and ask them to salute the flag, to sing "God save the King," to be loyal to our King and country; and the little ones of foreign extraction are glad to join our own children, and their parents are proud to see them participating in those exercises. But when on election day those little foreigners find that the mothers of other children go to the polls to exercise that great right of British subjects-the right to choose their rulers, and they come home full of pride in their adopted country and say, "Mother, everybody is going to vote to-day. In the country
we came from we had very little to do -with anything like this, but here everybody has the right to say who shall govern. Mother, have you been down to vote?" And that poor mother will have to say, "I am not allowed to vote. This flag which we are so proud to salute, this King whose life you are singing that God may prolong so he may, through this Parliament, continue to reign over us-that flag, that King and that Parliament have disfranchised me and I have no right to vote like other British subjects."
Shame !
Three times shame!

Let me tell you, Sir, that we are bringing humiliation to the hearts and minds of those youngsters that they will nevetr forget and never forgive, and we are bringing humiliation to the parents that they will never forget and never forgive. And what is it all for? I would like to be able to answer that question, but I cannot.
The policy of this great country should be, as we have been taught often during this session, to make the most of the foreigner in our midst, to confer upon him the right to vote, to exact from him all the duties of a citizen, so that we may have a better and a more united country. Not very long ago the hon. member for Fron-tenae (Mr. Edwards) quite properly initiated a discussion as to what we were doing for the children of our foreigners to put them on the same footing educationally with our own children; and every one was anxious that ways and means should be found to educate not only those children but the parents themselves in the principles of our Government and the ideals of our nation. The hon. member for South Perth (Mr. Steele) recently proposed a resolution calling upon all of us to get together and see what we could do for our foreign population, and he said that we were too slow in bringnig them into proper line with our national ideals and principles of government and were not making the most of their talents. Well, we were all willing to fall in line with the hon. member, and also with the hon. member for Frontenac, in doing whatever was possible to advance the interests of these foreigners, and so advance our own. But when, immediately after those fervent speeches, it comes down to the first practical test, we say to these foreigners, "Away with you! We know you not. No privilege is coming to you so long as we can keep it from you.

I submit, Sir, that it is not worth while for the minister and the Government to take those drastic steps for any results that they expect to get therefrom. I hope that their better judgment will prevail, and that the minister in charge of this Bill will withdraw this objectionable clause, so that every British subject in this country may be in a position on election day to exercise his God-given right to say who shall rule over him for the next five years.

Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to detain the committee at any great length, but I feel that it is my duty to supplement 'the powerful appeal we have just had from the hon. member for Cape Breton North (Mr. McKenzie), succeeding, as it does, to many others. I feel it is my duty to emphasize the central anomaly of this clause. I have neither the legal knowledge nor the desire to go into any detail on the matter. But it has been stated again and again that the ministry and their supporters are proposing to pass a clause whereby a negress married to a Mexican shall be able to vote in this British country under the British flag, while by the same clause that right will be denied to numerous women ootming from the countries of Europe, whether those countries are inhabited by our Allies or by those who were recently our enemies. And this is the twentieth year of the twentieth century!
It is an anachronism, it is an injustice, it is an absurdity; -and with all the power of voice and thought I protest against such legislation going on the statute book of a British 'country. It is a disgrace. If I had my way this session would last a good deal longer while every member who feels this in his blood made hlis protest, as we have tried to make it.
I endorse the first remarks which fell from my hon. friend from Dorchester (Mr. Cannon) last Thursday, when he said that it is impossible to exaggerate the importance of this question. It is important because it goes to the very fundamentals of the differences which have divided parties throughout the British Empire ever since franchise reform was spoken of. It goes to the very root of the matter, and it raises in acute form the difference between reaction or toryism on the one hand and progressive, democratic or liberal views upon the other. For any part, I am proud to he associated with 'those who stand on this matter for the progressive and the broad view as against the reactionary and restricted view. That is the question regarded from the political standpoint as a matter of justice and decency.
Now, one cannot be surprised at an honest Tory like my hon. friend from West Calgary (Mr. Tweedie supporting a clause like this, because he has told us whence he derives his information on electoral matters. He says that in matters of franchise and things relating to the constitution he would rather follow Edmund Burke than the humble individual now addressing this committee. But that was a very poor way to put the point. What he should have said was that he would rather follow Edmund Burke than the general opinion, as we had thought it was, of the whole of the electorate of Canada. I thought it was understood that we lived in a democratic country where Edmund Burke's views had long been forgotten. Mr. Chairman, I wonder if my hon. friend has really studied Mr. Burke or whether the particular quotation on which he based himself the other night was given to him by some one. I am not going into this question at length; I do not want to go into it, because I should be very sorry to be-called to order four times by the Chairman, or to be called to order at all. But I think it is perfectly germane to the argument that I am trying to present and perfectly germane to the discussion of this clause to show how it is perfectly natural for a hoary-headed Tory to vote for the narrow and restricted view upon this question, especially when he derives his inspiration from Edmund Burke.
Now, Edmund Burke was one of the most colossal figures that ever sat in the British House of Commons. But after all, he lived one hundred and forty years ago. While other persons referred to in the debate the other night lived a great deal longer time ago and were good instructors on morals, I have never heard that we went to either the New or the Old Testament for instruction on the electoral franchise. I do not know how elections were conducted in Judaea, but we do not go there for our inspiration on the franchise. However, let us see the kind of inspiration we should get by going to Edmund Burke. Mr. Burke made a famous speech upon this very question of the representation of the people in the House of Commons. I do not propose to read the speech, I need not say; but I will read two or three extracts from it. He said:
The reason for the Crown as it is, for the lords as they are, is my reason for the Commons-as they are, the electors as they are.
And what is the fact about the Commons and the electors when Edmund Burk lived?'
TMr. McKenzie.l

There were hardly any electors. The House of Commons was elected on a very narrow and restricted franchise under the dictation of the House of Lords. That is the condition under which Mr. Ed'mund Burke lived, and he argued for a continuance of that condition by saying he would have the Commons and the electors kept as they are, just as he wanted to keep the lords and the Crown as they were. I say that any one who derives his inspiration from that source would naturally vote for any clause restricting the franchise in any way imaginable. So Tories have always been; every successive extension of the suffrage has had to be wrung from them; has had to be beaten out of them. Now, let me give my hon. friend another quotation from his favourite and inspirer. Burke says again:
Now, I ask, what advantage do you And that the places which abound in representation possess over others in which it is more scanty, in security for freedom, in security for justice, or in any one of those means of procuring temporal prosperity and eternal happiness, the ends for which society was formed?
That is a beautiful passage to guide the deliberations of a democratic assembly in what we suppose to be the democratic country of Canada! And yet Edmund Burke is the inspirer of at least some of the thought on the other side of the House. Well, I repeat, it is no wonder that votes from that source will go to restricted franchise. Then, he ended that speech with the famous passage which begins:
I look with filial reverence on the constitution of my country.
The constitution was The King, to whom we are still all loyal; it was the House of Lords, and it was the House of Commons, created under a very narrow, restricted franchise, and unequal distribution, and at the bidding in many cases of the House of Lords. It was the day of rotten boroughs, the classes ruling and the people being told to be thankful that their temporal affairs and their eternal salvation were being looked after by their betters. That is the inspiration of my hon. friend from West Calgary, and it would be the inspiration of any one who had similar Tory proclivities coming down from so long ago.
But I am free to confess that I do not believe there are many Tories who would defend such a speech as that from which I have just quoted as applicable to present-day conditions. They ought to dissociate themselves, therefore, from the support of this clause, because after all, Mr, Chairman, for the last generation of
men in this country there has been no difference, practically speaking, on questions of franchise between the different sides of politics.
But if it he true that not many Tories would derive their inspiration from that source, what am I to say of my Liberal-Unionist friends? Are they going to vote under the inspiration of Edmund Burke? Are they going to vote for giving to a negress a right which they refuse to French women? Are they going to vote for that, and then go back to the broad prairies and the clear air and the broader thoughts of Western Canada and expect their views to be accepted by the electorate? I see mv hon. friend from Bow River (Mr. Halladay) in his place. I see my hon. friend from Strathcona (Mr. J. M. Douglas). There are very few Liberal Unionists in the Chamber. I see my hon. friend from Macdonald (Mr. Henders), and I see my hon. friend from Fraser Valley (Mr. Stacey). I cannot count any other Liberal Unionists on that side. But I should like to appeal to these hon. gentlemen, who have been influenced by Liberal traditions and who have Liberal views. I put it to them plainly, and to those who act with them; are they going to vote for a clause which confers electoral rights upon negresses married to Mexicans in this broad, free, democratic country and in this twentieth century, which rights they refuse alike to alien women and to women of our allies coming from Europe? Thlat is the sample question. I repeat that to vote for the clause is to vote for the enactment of an anachronism, an injustice and an absurdity.
There is no need to threaten the Government over the business; it will be very simple to have the clause dropped. We know that from what we have seen happen in the House in recent times. The other day, under the guidance of the minister, my hon. friend (Mr. Tweedie) wasted nearly a day of the time of this House when everybody who has the real interests of Canada at heart is trying to get to the end of the session-wasted it over an amendment. You know what happened to the amendment. At least, I do not think anybody does quite know-it disappeared; it is gone. All that happened was that my hon. friend from Neepawa (Mr. Davis), whom I should like to have had the honour of addressing on this question, rose and said:	Now, you had better drop this
thing-and dropped it was. They say that on the field of battle when men are in the

moment of defeat and panic they sometimes roar before they run. However that may be, the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Tweedie) the other day made a brave showing for sixty minutes; then he wandered out of the Chamber with the amendment which he had wasted a day over, in his back-tail pocket. There the amendment disappeared. They laughed best who laughed last in a matter of that kind. All that is necessary for any of my Liberal-Unionist friends who insist here that they should not support this thing, is not to vote against the Government-they will never get the chance of killing the Government in that way if I can trust recent experiences-but to tell the Government to kill the clause, and that will be done. The responsibility is a tremendous one. There is an old saying: "If you scratch a Russian, you will find a Tartar." Well, we have came to the time in this country when the people are asking: If you scratch a Unionist, do you find a Tory? That is a very serious question for my Liberal-Unionist friends to consider. I am very much afraid that this Government, having lost, one by one, their Liberal-Unionist representatives -to my great sorrow, we have a minister introducing this Franchise Act who has in his veins as good Liberal blood as ever flowed in Ontario-are bringing us to the position when the Unionism of the Government and the Liberalism of the Government will need a microscope to discover them and the broad reactionary Toryism of the'aggregation will stand out in bold relief. The country will make no mistake about what it is dealing with; it will say:	This
Government formed upon a fifty-fifty basis has lost the red political blood; it has passed into a state of anaemic and degraded Edmund Burke Toryism, and the country will put it where it belongs.
I should like, if it be not too late, to appeal to the minister and to the other members of the Government. What is going to be gained by insisting upon a piece of legislation such as this? Why not drop the clause? From the party point of view, whom do hon. gentlemen think they are going to gain? I do not care to go behind *the motives of those who support this monstrosity, for monstrosity it is tried by the single principle that I have endeavoured to lay down and emphasize. I found in the 1917 election that it was very doubtful, in many parts of the West at any rate, whether any party advantage was derived from the partial enfranchisement of women, that we had in that election. Men came to me and they said: 'fiDo you mean to tell me it 
is true that Mrs. So-and-So has a vote and *my wife has not?" I had to answer: "Yes, that is so." Then 'I knew what happened. Men who otherwise would have voted for me went straight to the ballot box and voted against me. From the party point of view, the proceeding is a very doubtful one. And the reason is not far to seek. The sense of justice and fairplay is so strongly ingrained in British peoples-I mean people under British institutions-that when an injustice is done, they will mark their reprobation of it by the first instrument that comes their way to handle, and I venture to think that though you debar women under this infamous clause, and those women possibly would vote against you, you will raise such a feeling amongst large numbers of your own supporters, male and female, that they will, by voting in another way, more than make up 9 p.m. for any gain you think you make -if you do think you make gain -by debarring certain women. But it is from the national point of view which has been so well put by the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria that I plead with the Government. I was very much pleased with a remark the hon. member made the other day. He said: The war is over; eighteen months have elapsed since the Armistice was signed; it is our sacred duty, a duty to which I would fain believe that every one of us in this chamber is anxious to contribute his quota, to reconstruct this country, not only in its financial affairs, in its industrial life, in its economic life, but in what is far more important than that, by healing the mental wounds of war, by giving our people no grievance, by leaving them no sense of wrong, by establishing conditions under which we shall know that we are in a democratic country because every one of us has equal rights and democratic privileges. That is the ground upon which I would make my chief appeal to the ministry to drop this clause even at this period.
My hon. friend (Mr. McKenzie), in his concluding words, did, far better than I could, that which I rose to my feet with the intention of doing. He pleaded with the Government not 'to give growing children a grievance, to leave no sense of grievance nor injustice, after all the harrowing times of war, in the mincSs oif any of out people. The Government are making a distinction in favour of the women of Mexico and Negresses as 'against women coming from France, Belgium and other European countries. The Government are inflicting an injury upon the fair name of Canada; they

are inflMing a wrong upon certain people; they are creating -a feeling of injustice; they are disgracing the statute book of this realm. I plead with the Government even now to see the error of their way and to drop this most iniquitous proposition. I shall have no hesitation whatever, but very great pleasure and pride, in voting with the hon. member for Waterloo North (Mr. Euler).

Just foT a few minutes I should like to protest against the extraordinary position taken by my hon. friend (Mr. M. Clark). He would sacrifice, as I understand fit, those people who came under this provision, provided, however, that the subclause shall not apply to any person bom upon the continent of North America. In order that he should carry his point with regard to the others, he rwould sacrifice these people. As a matter of expediency or otherwise, or compliance with the Naturalization Act, we understand that those bringing in this Bill have found it necessary or advisable, for this occasion only, to make this limitation with a proviso, however, which attaches to itself a very great deal of importance and which the liberal-minded gentleman who has just sat down argues against in a most extraordinary way. He would have these people, to whom this franchise is extended, cut out rather .than that those mentioned in the first part of the subclause should not he provided for .as he has seen fit to assert they tehould jbe. (This argument, therefore, of my hon. friend-I say this with all respect-nullifies itself. He has argued for the principle of the extension in the first part of 'the clause and absolutely and completely denied it in (the second. I must confess that I am unable to comprehend such reasoning. It would have been far better not to have ridiculed the Mexican and the Negress, hut, if you like, to have said that the Government were going too fax in extending the franchise to the Mexicans and the Negresses, although I do not .agree with him in that, provided they are intelligent people. But he has seen flit to ridicule their position and to say that the extension oi the franchise to .the Mexicans and Negresses is an absurdity in view of the first part of the clause. These pretty little jibes about scratching a Unionist and finding a Tory, and so forth, are very nice. But we do not have to scratch the farmers; they do that for themselves. I must confess that I think such remarks to be far from conducive to sane 141
and reasonable discussion of the subject. It is not very dignified to quote the great Burke in one breath and try to throw contempt and ridicule upon this side of the House in the- next. We know that Burke was a reactionary. We know of course that he stood for everything that was against the French revolution and seemed to be carried away by the Austrian princess who occupied the French throne at the time. But Burke nevertheless was an honourable . man; he was a great man. Like others, he made his mistakes, and it is for us to sift the grain from the chaff and to appreciate and profit by whatever was right in that which he proclaimed. The great lesson of Burke to posterity, as I understand it, i3 the fact that his eminently philosophical mind clarified the situation and was -above all things absolutely honest. He took some most extraordinary positions no doubt and was assailed by such men as Fox. But what he wrote regarding the sublime and beautiful will always appeal to us for the extraordinary and noble character of his mind and the loftiness of his conception, But I am well satisfied that the ministry, and the minister who is in charge of t-he Bill and who, as an hon. gentleman has well said, is a man of lofty and noble characteristics, have no personal motives in permitting the provision which this clause contains. And when the clause has served its purpose I am sure it will be repealed or amended.
After the next election.
Oh, oh.

pense-evil be to him who evil thinks. If I made a statement that hon. gentlemen opposite construe as in the nature of an admission, I confess that I did so in the innocence of my mind. The unworthy meaning which hon. gentlemen opposite take pleasure in attaching to that statement certainly did not occur to me nor, I believe, to any other hon. member on this side.
No.

Some people judge
others according to their own standards.

To the pure all things
are pure.

Hon. gentlemen opposite ascribe to us motives the imputation of which, were they circumstanced as we are, they would no doubt resent. Let not hon. gentlemen judge others by themselves unless their standards are a little higher than those of the persons whom they

subject. We have exactly the same considerations to take account of here to-day; the onlj difference is that we are dealing not witli breign policy hut with our policy at home We have even an identical case as respects every naturalized Jew affected by this legislation, the only possible difference is that instead of the rights of one Portuguese Jew as a British subject being effected - the rights of m'any naturalized jJewis ail'd thousands of other British subjects in this country are being invaded by the legislation which the [Government itself is seeking to force through. It cannot be d'enied that this section of the Bill subjects to a measure of indignity and thereby may deprive thousands of women, and many men of alien or foreign origin but who are British subjects, of rights which are given to others on the ground of their British citizenship. The section even takes away from thousands rights which have been already given to them ,ais British subjects by the Government. Let the committee understand that clearly. This Parliament, through its naturalization law, gives to these men and women, who to all intents and purposes are being disfranchised by subsection 2, the. right to be considered as British subjects. Parliament went farther than that, it passed an Act only two years ago giving every British subject, male or female, the right to the franchise. Why then does the Government at the present time deny to large numbers of persons a right which they have already given and which they profess to be willing to continue. I contend there is something here which all must stand up and contend for at the present time who are inter-jested in British justice, in British fair play, and in 1 maintaining in this (Dominion and especially throughout the British Empire principles of justice and all that we should wish to imply when we use the term "British .subject." I (make this further 'appeal to _ the Government either to give us substantial reasons why we should destroy the traditions which have led us to consider that being a British subject, implies the same treatment for one and all, or to listen to the plea that is now being made on behalf of those British subjects who will suffer indignity as a result of the Government's proposed action.
Let me again, Mr. Chairman, plead with [DOT]the Government, and with the minister, for the sake of their own honour as well as for the sake of justice in this matter, to do what at the outset they promised they

would do, and what they are on record in Hansard as having said would be the guiding principle of this Bill. If the Government fails to do that, then we might just as well understand at the moment that in this Bill, from one end to the other, we may expect evidences of the same kind of manoeuvres and of the same kind of deception-because that is what it is-as we have found in this particular instance. Every member of this House is interested in giving to the people of Canada a franchise in which they will have confidence. This Government has tampered with the franchise in the last five years as no Government under the sun has ever tampered with a franchise, and they have got so into the habit of passing laws interfering with the rights of the people in the matter of their votes that it now seems but a relatively small thing to deny to thousands of people a fundamental right which, in the Government's own words, they profess to be giving to every one.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have heretofore, during the progress of this debate in committee discussed this clause at considerable length and I do not know that I could, at this late date, afford any more information upon the subject than is now in possession of hon. gentlemen. I must say, however, that I think it rather a late hour for my hon. friend from Red Deer, and also my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition, to come forward with a display of indignation, which I am satisfied is but a mockery of their real feelings, in an attempt to show that the Government, in the clause now under discussion, has in any way endeavoured to deceive either the House or the public in regard to the proposals contained in this Bill. Personally I do not think I ever heard my hon. friend from Red Deer labour over a question as hard as he laboured to-night. He certainly spoke under great excitement and with, great force; but the indignation which he was able to command in regard to what he called the quadroon vote and the Mexican vote, that was going to come into this country from the United States on more favourable terms than should be applied to the women of other countries was, in my judg* ment, the height of absurdity. My hon. friend from Red Deer knows, or should know-because he has lived long enough in Canada to know,-that this country is not favoured with any emigration of the negro population of the South, nor yet of the state of Mexico farther to the South-we have practically no residents of that part

of the globe in this country. It is true that in former days we had a considerable southern population who came into Canada to escape slavery and to choose freedom. But that population has been decreasing year by year in every riding in Canada where it existed, and within measurable distance, in all likelihood we shall have none of it, .climatic conditions being the chief reason for this; and there is no Mexican population in Canada. So that when my hon. friend says that one reason why he will oppose this clause is because we are going to permit the quadroon and the Mexican woman to come here on better conditions than women from Europe, the matter to my mind resolves into an absolute absurdity quite unworthy of my hon. friend.
Now, with regard to the statement of the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King). Why, my hon. friend would have the House believe that in something I said on behalf of the Government I misled the House. My hon. friend knew every line in t'he Bill before it was introduced into this House at all. I especially requested a conference with him, and that conference was held several days before the Bill was introduced. That very question in section 29 was discussed between us, and I tell the House my hon. friend took no exception to the clause. Furthermore, Mr. Chairman, on the day upon which the Bill obtained its first reading-the first day upon which the Bill came from the printer-I myself gave him a copy of the measure. Many days elapsed before the second reading of the measure; from time to time that step was put off at the request of my hon. friend in order that he and his friends might have a chance of studying the Bill. He knew every line and every clause of it, and so far as my knowledge goes he has taken no exception to it until this late date.
Now, how about the attitude of the House in regard to this matter? This very Parliament, elected in 1917, has on two occasions affirmed the principle and affirmed it unanimously, what does my hon. friend from Red Deer think of that statement? He was a member of the House in 1918, and I say he affirmed that principle-at all events he did not divide the House or vote or speak against it. He was a member of the House in- 1919 when the By-Elections Act was passed which contained that very same clause. I say again that he affirmed the measure because he did not vote against or speak against it on either occasion, and that the Bill received
the unanimous approval of the House. Therefore, I repeat, the same clause was unanimously affirmed twice, once in 1918, and once in 1919-although I may say that in 1918 that special clause-
Hear, hear.

speechtext: -as to the women born in North America was not included, but was subsequently included. Hon. members opposite know why. Ask my hon. friend from' North Essex (Mr. Kennedy) or my hon. friend from George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs). At their request the clause was inserted. I think it is a fair and reasonable clause; I think it is a good clause and that it ought to be put there. But at all events we affirmed the principle in 1918 unanimously; we affirmed it in 1919 unanimously. Does the minister

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Acting Solicitor General himself may say that we are putting on mock indignation, but he does not seem to travel very easily when he tries to answer the arguments which are put forward why this clause should be struck out. He tells my leader (Mr. Mackenzie King) that he should not complain. He says:	I had an interview
with you before the Bill was brought down; I mentioned this clause 29; why did you not object? Why, Mr. Chairman, how could you expect the leader of the Opposition to discuss a measure which he had not had time to read or to analyse, when the minister himself confesses, with the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen), that if the words as printed in the Bill conveyed the meaning attributed to them by my hon. friend from North Waterloo (Mr. Euler), that had not been the intention of the Government and they would have to be changed? I want to quote my hon. friend's words to show what was the position of the Government when this Bill was being discussed, because with all the strength of the opinion of officers of the House behind them and all the legal talent that they could muster on the other side, evidently the Bill as brought down did not convey exactly what the Government had in mind. On May 5, my hon. friend from North Waterloo' having pointed out that this clause was not a fair clause and that it would disfranchise certain people, the Acting Solicitor General as reported on page 2126 of unrevised Hansard, said:
The question raised hy my hon. friend from North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) is not without some complexity. Under the Bill as originally introduced-clause 29, subclause 2-the intention of the Government in framing the clause was hardly expressed by the language used, as was pointed out on the second reading of the Bill hy the Minister of the Interior.
Now, it does not behoove the Acting Solicitor General to reproach my leader with not having jumped at the meaning of the clause when the Government itself could not express its view .in the legislation which they were submitting. The proof of the pudding is in the eating; the Acting Solicitor General has since brought down an amendment with a view to correcting the clause. He went on to say:
The effect of the clause as originally drawn, and now printed in the Bill, would be to disqualify a certain number of people in this country who had heretofore become British subjects by operation of law. The people who would have been thus disqualified, were the section allowed to remain in its present condition, were the wives and children of those who had come to

this country from foreign countries and obtained naturalization in Canada during their minority. As the committee is well aware, the wife of an alien who becomes naturalized in this country, under our law, becomes a British subject. The wife did not have to appear and obtain the certificate of naturalization-she became a British subject by operation of law by the fact of her marriage. Under the old common law idea she merged her existence, her identity became merged in her husband, and by operation of law she became a British subject. So it was also with the children who were minors at the time the parent became a British subject. Not so with the children who had come to the age of twenty-one years. They retained their original citizenship until they should themselves apply for naturalization in this country. My hon. friend from North Waterloo was, I think, the first to point out, during the debate on the second reading of this Bill, that the clause as drawn, had the effect of depriving a certain number of British subjects of the right to the franchise. The Minister of the Interior very promptly informed the House that such was not Intended-that if that were the interpretation of the language of the section it did not convey the intention of the Government-and he promised the House that when the Bill came up again an amendment would he introduced to give effect to the intention of the Government, which was to maintain the right of those persons who had become naturalized by operation of law to all their rights, including the right of the franchise.
That is plain English; it could not be plainer. Yet the Acting Solicitor General now reproaches my leader because he did not, before the Bill was submitted to the House, find out that this clause disfranchised a certain number of persons. He says further:
Now the amendment which I have just had the honour of moving is intended to cure that defect in the section as It is printed in the present Bill, and I would ask the committee to examine the language of that amendment. In my humble opinion the language of the amendment does cure the defect; but if there be any doubt on that point I have no hesitation in saying the Government has no desire to create a doubt on the subject, and we will employ any language that may be necessary to make the matter plain and free from doubt.
What do we ask, Sir? We ask that this subsection be struck out. The Acting Solicitor General answers by saying that there are hardly any negroes in this country. Well, that is not the point; it is the principle that counts. Let me give an example. Suppose an ignorant negro woman comes from the South. She is the wife of a man who is a British subject. A refined woman, highly educated, comes to Canada from France or Belgium. She speaks the language of the country. Sihe employs this negiro woman as a servant. People of high standing in the community entrust to this French woman the training and instruction

of their children. Election day comes, and this French woman, trained in literature, well versed in sciences, her husband a British subject, is deprived of her right to vote because she-was born in France; and the negro wench who scrubs her floors goes down to the poll and has a voice in saying what shall be the fate of this country. Is there any sense in that? I say, no.
When people who come to this country want to analyse what rights they are going to get, they are not going to take the census to find out how many women of any given national origin there are in this country; but they are going to take the law and proceed by comparison, and they will find out the injustice-yes, I say further, the iniquity-of this legislation on the continent of North America. Hon. gentlemen opposite jeer at the fact that my friends bring up the case of the Mexicans. These people, however few or many come here, do not speak the language of the country, while the French and the Belgians do; but the former can go to the poll and vote, while these women of higher education, more refinement, speaking the language of this country, are going to be deprived of the right to vote. What answer do we receive? " Pretended indignation." "Mockery." I do not think that is fair. If the Government are sincere when they call upon us to discuss this question, or if they are sincere when they say they find any good purpose in inserting this provision, let them give us reasons, not words, not opinions. This clause must have something behind it. The answer is: There are very few of these people. Well, if few, why disfranchise them? If there are a large number of them, then you are committing an injustice on those people and you ought not to disfranchise them. My opinion-I expressed it before- is this: I think there are a great number of these women who ought to have the right to vote. But the Government fear less the judgment of a Nigger or a Mexican than they fear the judgment of educated, refined and cultured women. The feelings of those women, who come from France, Belgium or any other of the Allied countries, are such that any acts of autocracy as are being committed daily they would fear more than the other women would. This is an additional method of endeavouring to make votes as the cost of an injustice. My hon. friends opposite claim that they want to give a fair franchise; but if we make any suggestion or point out anything that we think unfair, we are jeered and laughed at.
The only reason I can think of for the way in which they dismiss our arguments and our appeals to cut out this clause is that they fear that some votes may go against them. My hon. friends might just as well come out boldly and in a manly way. Why do you not disfranchise every man and every woman in this country who will not vote for the Union Government-or what used to be a Union Government? Then, possibly we would not have to scratch in order to find out what you want? You dare not do this openly; but you want, by small cuts here and there to try to disfranchise as many open-minded, patriotic people as you dare, in order to gain a political advantage; you are depriving these people of the most sacred right vested in a subject, namely, the right to vote.
Some of my friends argue that this is a privilege. It is not a privilege; it is a right. When I come here and acquire British citizenship, the only way in which I can exercise my right as a citizen is by going to the polls and saying in what way my country shall be run. I want to have a vote and a voice in the legislation of this country and to be able to say who shall be my representative, who shall voice my
10	p.m. views in the Parliament of Canada. The time when the franchise is being exercised is the only time in a man's existence when every man is equal before the law; that is the only time when the poor man can walk up to the poll alongside of the millionaire and say: " For once you have not the best of me; my vote is the same value as yours." Now you are going to deprive these people of the most sacred right they have. You say: That is a privilege we give them. I say: It is a right to which they are entitled, and it is a crime to deprive them of that right.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I just want to answer my hon. friend's question.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: A point of order has been raised by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Michael Clark). I would certainly agree with the hon. member that the House of Commons would not be in order in discussing a Bill introduced into the Ontario Legislature by any Government, but I think it is in order for the hon. minister (Mr. Rowell) to refer to one of these Bills by way of comparison.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: In answer to my hon. friend, the clause which I understood was in the Bill was one which provided that a woman who was naturalized by operation of law was required to apply for and obtain a certificate that she possessed the qualifications necessary for naturalization before she became entitled to vote.

That is not what my hon. friend said at all. My hon. friend quoted a section of the Bill, which he said'was section 2, and which he also said was contained in the Drury Bill of 1920. The Drury Bill of 1920 does not contain any ouch section as section 2, eo that my hon. friend is absolutely wrong in quoting that- as section 2 of the Drury Bill?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Will my hon. friend tell me if there is such a clause in the Drury Bill?	[DOT]

As what?
Mr. ROWE'LL:	Which requires that a
woman, naturalized by operation of law, must apply for and obtain a certificate to show that she is possessed of the qualifications necessary for naturalization before she becomes entitled to vote.

I cannot say it is in this Bill at all. It may be there-I want to be fair to this discussion. My hon. friend quoted
a section which he said was a section of the Drury Bill but which was not a section of the Drury Bill. I do not deny that a section in these terms is there.
Read the Bill.

There are sections
within the Bill referring to former sections and former Acts and I do not know positively if they contain the restrictions which .my hon. friend says they do, but I know certainly that the sections which he calls the sections of the Bill of 1920 are not the sections of the Drury Act of 1920.

I would like to ask the
President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell) a question. He has referred to the Franchise Act that the Drury Government has introduced into the Ontario Legislature. Can he tell the committee if that Act contains a clause of the discriminatory character of this subsection 2 of section 29?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am very glad to answer my hon. friend's question, It does not contain the provision relating to North American women, and the reason why that clause was put in, as my hon: friend will know, was to meet the case of the wives of American settlers in Western Canada, whereby women from the United States brought up under similar institutions, many of them having exercised the franchise and being accustomed to vote, and who are naturalized by operation of law, are not required to obtain a certificate. It was put in to meet the condition of the wives of American settlers in Western Canada. I am sure my hon. friend would not like to strike it out upon that ground.

I wish to take exception to the rather sarcastic way in which the Acting Solicitor General treated the committee this evening as regards declarations made by members in the debates which took place during the two sessions on this question while the franchise was discussed. My hon. friend said that it was an absurdity to discuss this question as we are discussing it this evening when as a matter of fact it was never challenged by a vote in the House. Now it has been fairly established, much to the discomfiture of my hon. friend the Acting Solicitor General, that the provision was challenged upon two occasions. On the first occasion a vote, not a division, was taken in the House.

Now, I grant this to the Acting Solicitor General so far as the Franchise Act is concerned; in Oirdex that no ultra-loyal members may be heard complaining here or to his constituents that I moved an 'amendment which is going Ito let these people in, that the floodgates are to be opened for their admission, I am content, so far as this amendment is concerned, as are hon. members on this side of the 'House, that the ten-year clause should be lived up to. And it is. .provided that no disability imposed by the said paragraph (B) shall prevent any person, possessed of the qualifications which would have entitled such person to naturaliza-' Ron prior to the year 1914, applying to a judge for a certificate that he was so qualified,
