speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
As the discussion has
proceeded on clause 29 I think the committee has been- incidentally entertained with a general discussion of the amendment now moved by my hon. friend (Mr. Pardee) in concrete form. I think that the amendment is objectionable; first, because it is really an amendment to the Naturalization Act, or ought to be, rather than an attempt to amend the Franchise Act. What is sought by the amendment now before the committee is a change in our present naturalization law which will permit of a dual system of naturalization in the country, first, in part, the Naturalization Act, which has special requirements enacted by this House in 1919, and, second, a naturalization law limited in its operation to the Dominion of Canada, practically putting back the law so far as the franchise is concerned to the law as we found it in Canada prior to 1914.
Are you not, in this Bill, changing the Naturalization Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: No, I do not think we are changing it.
Certainly.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
What we are doing is
recognizing its full force and application.

Not by the
amendment which the minister (Mr. Guthrie) moved.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes, for this reason;
the people with whom subsection 2 would deal were British subjects by operation of law, and wrere people who were not affected by the Naturalization Act. But the object of the present amendment is to void the plain enactment which this House made in 1919, and on that ground it is objectionable. If my hon. friend deems that our Naturalization Act is improper or that it should be amended, he should bring forward a Bill to amend the Naturalization Act-and I doubt very much whether after its solemn pronouncement on the question one year ago, the House would feel inclined to amend the Naturalization Act.
Now, the amendment is objectionable in form and would likewise be objectionable in its operation and in its result. I am free to speak for myself on this subject, and I say that my experience of people I know in Ontario of German nationality who have lived in this country thirty, forty dr fifty years has not been such as to lead me to believe that these people are entitled to the franchise, particularly at the present time. I would not be in favour of the proposal on that ground. I state the result of my own personal experience in regard to the matter. I am satisfied that the Imperial Naturalization Act was passed with a ten-year limitation against persons of alien enemy countries and adopted in Canada, Australia and the other dominions only after the fullest consideration and for the express purpose of seeing to it that people of enemy nationality should not, for a period of at least ten years succeeding the war, be treated as other subjects. I do not believe that the amendment moved by my hon. friend meets the situation in Canada.
I grant that there may be many worthy people who have resided in this country for many years and who under normal conditions might be entitled to the franchise or to have exceptions made of their cases. But this also must be remembered; these people have been pretty careless in the past; they have been negligent of their rights. If citizenship is the great boon which we believe it to be-and British citizenship is certainly a great boon-these people have been hopelessly careless in that they did not see to it that they became

British citizens during these thirty, forty or fifty years. 'They have waited a long time. They have enjoyed all the protection given to British subjects upon the assumption that they had become such. If they have waited twenty, thirty or forty years in that condition, I think no great injustice will be done to them if they are allowed to remain ten years longer in order that they may comply with the law which this Parliament and the Parliaments of the other dominions saw fit so recently to pass. For these reasons, Mr. Chairman-and these are broad, general principles I am stating -and for the reasons which I stated on another occasion during the course of the discussion on this Bill, o<n behalf of the Government I ask the committee to reject this amendment.

It had not been my intention to make any remarks on this amendment, but I do so now, in order to take issue with one or two statements made by the Acting Solicitor General (Mr. Guthrie). But before I do that, I think it would be fair, although the question has been discussed before by myself and others, to review the situation exactly as it exists so that members of the committee may vote with at least a fair measure of information on the question.
There are, as has been stated, in my constituency as well as in many others, a great many people of what may now be known as former enemy alien birth, who have lived in Canada for many years-many more years than the ten years now spoken of in the Naturalization Act-men. who have lived here for twenty, thirty, fifty, sixty and in one case that I know of, seventy years, who are not to-day in a position to prove that they are British subjects and who may perhaps, technically not be British subjects. I want to make this perfectly plain: you are in this particular case not only dealing with people who are not British subjects; you are dealing with some people who aTe British subjects but have no means of proving that they are such. We have men in my riding who were in this country before Confederation and^hc took the oath of allegiance. They came from Germany. They are to-day, in my opinion, British subjects, perhaps even in law, but they have absolutely nothing to show that they are British subjects. They have no naturalization papers, and unfortunately theTe appears to be no record anywhere of the fact that they did take the oath of allegiance.
Does the taking of the oath of allegiance make a man a British subject?

It does not now, but 1
think it did before Confederation.
Did it ever make a man a British subject?
I am not certain, but I believe it did before Confederation.
What makes him a British subject, then?

Now, we have those who thought themselves British subjects; we have those who, I believe, are British subjects but who are unable to show that they are such, and we have others who, whether you call it negligence or something else, never did become naturalized. I do not want to dwell on this, but I dto want to say in reply to what the Acting Solicitor General has just said, that his experience has been unfortunate; he does not believe that these people should be allowed to become naturalized until the lapse of another ten years. In that statement my hon. friend is in direct issue with his leader, the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden). I have not the words of the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) before me, but I can give them in effect. He stated at the Peace Conference, and he stated in this House, that there were a great many people in this country who were bom in enemy alien countries who were worthy of naturalization, and he, together with the President of the Council (Mr. Rowell) placed himself on record' at the Peace Conference as declining to support a suggestion made by representatives of other parts of the Empire that people of enemy alien birth should not be allowed naturalization for another ten years after the conclusion of the war. Those were the sentiments of the Prime Minister of Canada, and in order to prove that those were his sentiments, we need simply go to his acts in 1917. I have said this before, but I will say it again, because I think it ought to be said, that it is fair to consider the fact that in the year 1917, when, perhaps, we may say that the war was at its worst phase, the Government of this country passed, under powers given by Parliament, Orders in Council under which it was possible to make Canadian citizens of those people who are now under discussion under the amendment of the hon. member for Lambton West (Mr. Pardee).
In what way?

If the hon. member will
have patience, I will come to that now.. .This was the method that was to be followed: These men could go to a judge in the ordinary way; they could prove to his satisfaction, or not, as the case might be, that they were worthy of being naturalized. In my particular constituency, in the city of Kitchener, some 93 of them went to the judge, were approved as being worthy of naturalization, and then their applications were forwarded to the Secretary of State in order that the process of naturalization might be completed. There certainly was no object in passing those Orders in Council if it was never intended that any use should be made of them. I cannot for the life of me, see why those Orders in Cbuncil were passed before the elections of 1917 if it was not the intention that the powers under those Orders in Gouncil should be exercised. Yet, when the applications of those 93 people were sent to the Secretary of State, for some reason or other, although the machinery was there to make them- Canadian citizens, British subjects, they were not given that naturalization. I say that to prove that, in the opinion of the Prime Minister, provision should be made for the naturalization oi such people, and such provision was made which was afterwards nullified by the Act which was passed by the British Government and which was followed by the Naturalization Act of 1919 which was passed with the "ten-year" clause in order to meet the wishes of the British people, but not the wishes of the Prime Minister of Canada.
The Acting Solicitor General (Mr. Guthrie) said that if those people did not obtain naturalization in the long period oi time during which they were in Canada, they were guilty of negligence, and he assumed from that, that because those people were negligent, they did not deserve to obtain naturalization now. I do not see much force in that argument, for this reason amongst others. The minister will know, because he has some of these people in his riding, that in former years, matters of naturalization were not considered of as much importance as they are now, and it was perfectly natural that such should be the case. Those people had lived there for many years; they had had their names on the voters' lists from year to year; they had served on municipal councils; 'some of them, so far as I know, may have stood for Parliament; I do not know that for certain, but it would not have been

thought out of place if they had done so, because it was felt amongst all classes of people, including those horn in England, Scotland, Wales and Ireland, that those people were just the same as any other people in the county of Waterloo. They discharged their duties as citizens just the same as anybody else; there was no difference; and to show that such was the case, there was an understanding between the two parties, the Liberal and the Conservative parties, that when election time came, no man was ever to be challenged on the score of his nationality. It was taken for granted that if a man's name was on the voters' list, he was a citizen properly qualified to vote. So the matter went on. Under those conditions, it was surely not to be wondered at, especially when many of those men had taken the oath of allegiance, that they did not know the law so fully as to know that they must complete the operation by obtaining their papers. It was not be wondered at that they did not do anything further when they were enjoying all the rights of citizenship and when nobody was making any objection of any kind. It is those people who are included under the amendment, and it is to those people that we feel naturalization should be given. You are now willing to give men naturalization who calme fronn former alien enemy countries if they live here for another ten years. Why in the name of reason and ordinary common sense should it not be counted to the credit of those men that they have already lived he're ten years, or three or four or even five times ten years? Ilf it is going to be right to give naturalization ten years from now to men who, perhaps, came to this country in 1913 directly from Germany, are you going to make any exception against, the man who has lived here thirty or forty years?
While I do not want to appeal to sentiment at all, it is a fact that amongst those men to whom you now refuse the franchise for another ten years, although they have lived in this country so many years already, were men who had sons in this war. The Acting Solicitor General has made some rather strong statements that T resent; he has practically said that he would trust very few of those men who came here from Germany many years ago. I take issue with him on that, and while this is not altogether pertinent to the discussion, I want to say this on behalf of many of the people whom I consider I represent, although today they are not technically British subjects. We had in the riding of North Water-

loo a very difficult situation which some hon. members may realize. There were men there who, if they did not enlist, were criticised as slackers or' worse than that, and some hon. members who served in the war probably know this to he the case, that if a man who bore a German name went overseas, he was under a certain degree of suspicion until he proved undeniably that he was all right. Those men were, if I may use the expression, in many cases between the devil and the deep sea.
If they did not enlist, they were slackers or worse than that, and if they enlisted they were spies. This Parliament could now take a step that would restore, at least to some extent, a feeling of confidence that has disappeaied in some parts of this country because of unjust suspicion and Acts by previous Parliaments. I am not going to make recriminatiohs with regard to the War-time Elections Act. I have done that before, I think very moderately. That Act: was wrong; it deprived honest British subjects of the franchise; but I want to say this to the Government, that the war is over, and surely you could do
11	p.m. no better service to this country than to try to heal the wounds of war and to unite together into one people all Canadian citizens, no matter whether they come from England, Ireland, Scotland, or even from Germany, as long as they show they are worthy of being Canadian citizens.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It is not my intention to undertake to reply to my hon. friend (Mr. Euler). I have only two observations to make. The first is that up to date, neither this Parliament nor, do I believe, any legislative assembly has in a general Franchise Act conferred the franchise upon others than British subjects. This Act deals only with the franchise, and if my hon. friend's amendment is germane to this Act, it would mean in effect that we were conferring the franchise upon those who were not British subjects; that is a . proposal we cannot accept. If the effect of the amendment is to naturalize these men then it must pertain to the Naturalization law, and that is a question which should be dealt with under the Naturalization Act.
I rose to say that I have now a copy of the Drury Bill of 1920 which I did not have before me when I last spoke, and my hon. friend would not accommodate me with a copy.

-and that she has personally appeared and satisfied me

speechtext: Order. I must remind hon. gentlemen who desire to be heard that they should do the committee the honour of rising in their places and addressing the Chair. The hon. gentleman said that if I had sent the Bill across he would have told me what it meant. He introduced section 29 and he did not know what it meant. I am not disputing what the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell) said in regard to the points he raised in reference to the two Bills, but if he will go back and refer to the Bills of 1918 and 1919 he may find that what he said is practically correct. In the draft Bill of the Drury Government it will be found that former sections have been enacted in an obscure way and you would have to refer to the laws of 1918 and 1919 to see what the effect of some of these sections was. I did not have those laws before me. What the bon. gentleman said was, that he was quoting from a definite Bill when in fact he was not quoting from it and that was what I rose to point out.

The hon. member for
West Middlesex (Mr. D. C. Ross) has told us that he was discussing this matter frankly. The hon. member neglected to refer to the fact that he repeatedly said that he had the Drury Bill of 1920 before him and that he could not see the clause in question.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

Well, Mr. Chairman, I shall certainly bow to your ruling. A comparison was made between a bill introduced in the Ontario Legislature and a certain portion of the clause under discussion and
I presume that was why the reference to that Bill was regarded as pertinent. However, I shall bow to your ruling and not discuss that any further. I thank you.

I have every sympathy with the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) along certain lines. I have a great many German-born people in my riding who were misled by friends of the hon. member and who for many years, and perhaps up to the present time, or certainly until the beginning of the war, thought they were British subjects. In my riding these men were led as lambs to the slaughter, and were sworn by the ordinary oath of allegiance by magistrates appointed by the province of Ontario under the old regime. They were told they were British subjects and they in many cases 'believed it and continued to believe it up to the present time. But that does not make them British subjects in any sense of the word, and that is the only class of men to whom the hon. member's remarks would have any reference to at all. I have them in my riding as well as he has, and I have every sympathy with the men who were misled. The great majority of these people many years ago learned that this did not constitute the ordinary form of naturalization. They knew what the hon. member for North Waterloo knew, that every man who was naturalized under the Act before the beginning of the war could have obtained, as he can obtain to-day, a certificate that he was properly naturalized. My hon. friend can apply to the Secretary of State and obtain for the county of Waterloo the name of every German, Turk, or native of any country who has been naturalized within that county. He knows that as well as I do.
Is the hon. gentleman (Mr. Arthurs) trying to give the impression that I said anything to the contrary?
Yes, the hon. gentleman did give me that impression. He said that many men could not find out whether or not they were naturalized.
I said they had no proof.

The hon. gentleman said that many men in his county could not find out whether they were or were not

naturalized. Now he trikes the apposite side and says that he did not intend to give the impression to this House that they could not find out whether they were properly naturalized or not. I make the assertion now that any German or foreigner in Canada can very easily find out whether he has or has not been naturalized. It is open to any member of this House or to any person in Canada to find out whether he has been naturalized or not.
Will the hon. gentleman say that they could do that if they were naturalized before Confederation?
There was no naturalization before Confederation.
Will tney be recognized as British subjects if they were here before Confederation, or will they have any difficulty in proving it in order that they may vote?

My hon. friend was not referring to men .who are long since dead. He was referring to men who were in Canada and whose naturalization should or could have been conferred upon them since Confederation. The number of people who were here before Confederation would be so small as to be absolutely negligible in the argument. As I said before, as far as these men were concerned, I have a great deal of sympathy with them. Not long ago one of these men wrote to me saying that he had the naturalization papers issued by the province of Ontario and this man believed until the beginning of the war that he was a British citizen. But the amendment proposed by the hon. member for West Lambton (Mr. Pardee)-and hon. members on this side had no means of knowing what it was excepting by hearing it read by the hon. member-would have conferred upon the wives of all men who believe themselves to be citizens of Canada before or since the war the privilege of voting. It would not only have conferred that right upon the wives but would have conferred it upon the men themselves. In other words the amendment of the hon. member (Mr. Pardee) if adopted would allow these men-who before the war made no serious attempt to become British subjects-to have the privilege of voting. I do not think that is my hon. friend's intention, but that is the practical effect of the amendment he has moved.

I would like to correct
what the hon. member for Parry Sound says by quoting from the Order in Council itself:

The minister observes further that many persons of alien enemy origin who came to Canada many years ago, during infancy, and have grown up believing themselves to be British subjects, now that questions of nationality are being carefully scrutinized, find it impossible to show that they have become British subjects, although they have voted and held municipal positions for many years. Many others believe that they became British subjects through the naturalization of their parents, but they are unable to prove it because the records are not available.
That is from the Order in Council itself.
i Mr. ARTHURS: In reply to that I would repeat what I said before, that the records are available to any member of this House.
i Mr. PARDEE: The Government do not know that.
1 Mr. ARTHURS: The Government does know it.
Why did they make that *statement in the Order in Council, if such is the case??

These records are available to members of Parliament. I know that in my riding I asked for the returns showing the number of alien persons who have been naturalized in the district of [DOT]Parry Sound, and the records as far back as the year 1867, which I believe to be complete, were produced. I believe that on any similar question any hon. gentleman could obtain exactly the same records. So faT as the children -are concerned, it is a very minor matter; the trouble is with these cases with which I sympathize myself. I have a great deal of sympathy with the class of men who have been unwittingly misled; ibut the adoption of the amendment suggested by the hon. member for Lamb-ton will include a lot of men who' never had any deshe at all to become British citizens.

To read clause 29 intelligently we must bear in mind that up to now the discussion has been carried on in connection with two different classes of electors. The first class are the women and children who have become naturalized British subjects by operation of law; and the second class are the men who have received the privileges of British subjects in Canada for a certain period of years, but who, owing to certain particular or special reasons, have not in hand to-day certificates of naturalization and therefore are not to be considered as British subjects. These men-according to the naturalization law as it stands and reads to-day-would not be in

a position to <be naturalized for a period of ten years to come. The first class of people -that is the women and children-were disposed of by the amendment proposed by the member for North Waterloo which was voted down by the committee.
We are now dealing with the second class of people. The member for West Lambton proposed an amendtnent whereby any citizen of this country who has been living in Canada for at least ten years, and would be entitled to naturalization, would have the power, when an election takes place, to go before a judge and secure from that judge a certificate and, having done so, be entitled to cast his ballot. The amendment is to cover the case of the men to whom I referred: at the beginning of my remarks. The Acting Solicitor General very briefly answered the hon. gentleman (Mr. Pardee) by saying that it was absolutely impossible for the Government to accept that amendment because it meant an amendment to the Naturalization Act itself. We have heard, since the discussion of clause 29 began in this House several ministers telling us that it was absolutely impossible to touch the Naturalization Act because that Act was a piece of legislation passed by the Imperial Parliament, and adopted by the various Dominions giving the right to every British subject within the Empire the privileges of British citizenship throughout that Empire. The Acting Solicitor General says that what the hon. member (Mr. Pardee) proposes is absolutely unacceptable because it means laying our hands on this Naturalization law, and when the Minister refers to the Naturalization law he has in mind, if I understand him correctly, the law of 1919. The argument of the minister is either good or bad. If that argument is good it ought to cover all cases; if it is bad it ought to be rejected by the committee. I claim, Mr. Chairman that that argument is unsound, because this committe, led by him as adopted the second paragraph of clause 29 and that is a direct amendment to, and an express alteration of, the Naturalization Law of our country. According do the Naturalization Act of 1919 the wives of British subjects in this country are British, subjects. Furthermore the minor children were naturalized by the fact that their father was naturalized, and when they become of age are British subjects possessing all the rights of British subjects. I say that if the naturalization law of our country remains as it reads to-day, and if no other law was introduced into this Parliament, these women and these children would be entitled to vote. This is not only my personnel interpretation but it is, I think, that
of the highest authority in this House as far as Parliamentary procedure and Parliamentary precedents are concerned, I mean the Minister of Justice. (Mr. Doherty). The Minister of Justice has discussed this question before the committee, and if you refer to unrevised Hansard, page 2136, you will find that, speaking on this subject, in answer to a question he spoke, he said:
Mr. Doherty: There are a class of people from whom the vote to which they would otherwise be entitled is taken by this Act.

Hear, hear.
Mr. Cannon: And from the wives and the children?
Mr. Doherty: If this Act had not stepped in, these women having become British subjects by marriage, or the children having become British subjects by the naturalization of their fathers would have had a vote.
Hear, hear.

This is the declaration of the Minister of Justice who is the highest legal official in this House, a colleague .of the Minister of Militia, (Mr. Guthrie) and that declaration is a contradiction as flagrant as possible of the declaration just made by the Minister of. Militia. On the one side here is a minister who said: If there was no Franchise Act these women and these children would have a right to vote. On the other hand, when the hon. member for Lambton wishes to give at least some portion of justice to a class of our population the Minister of Militia replies: I refuse to accept that amendment, because by accepting it' I would alter the Naturalization Act. This House is entitled to better treatment from the Government. The Minister of Militia has no right to amend the Naturalization Act to suit his own purposes and the purposes of the Government on the one hand, and, on the other hand, to refuse the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Lambton because it does not suit his or their purposes any further. We have already amended the Naturalization Act, and in saying that I base myself on the declaration made in this House by the Minister of Justice; and he cannot deny it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Will my hon. friend
allow me? There is nothing in what he quoted as having been said by me which involves that there is any amendment to the Naturalization Act in the fact that these women and children were refused the vote. I did say that if that provision had not withdrawn their right to vote they would have had it. Why? Because if that right had not been withdrawn from them, this present Act would simply have said that

every British subject had such a right. But the class that he is now discussing is a class of people who are not British subjects. The distinction seems t-o me to be perfectly clear.

The Minister of Justice
says that the distinction is perfectly clear. Well, he may be very grateful that his sight is as good as that; mine is not. I say that the Minister of Justice declared in this House that if paragraph 2 of clause 29 had not been introduced these women and children would have had the right to vote; and to take away that right to vote that they had as British subjects-and they were British subjects according to our Naturalization law as it existed-the. Government had to change the existing law.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I never said that.
Thait inference, I can logically draw from the remarks made by him.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. gentleman can draw that inference, belt whether he can do so logically is another question.

Therefore I say that the Minister of Militia has no right to bring before this committee as a sound argument the fact that if the amendment brought in by the hon. member for Lambton was adopted it would in a way alter the provisions of the Naturalization Act. That Act, when it did not suit their purpose has been put aside already by the Government. - I think this matter is very clear and there cannot be any discussion on it. The Minister of Justice gets up and says: I did not express any opinion that these opinion were given the vote by the Naturalization Act. I know they are not. The Naturalization Act does not give the vote; but it dbes give British citizenship. And the Acting Solicitor General (Mr. Guthrie) as a Minister oif the Crown gave his pledge before this House and before the country that the qualifications to be an elector under this new Franchise Act would be British citizenship within certain limitations as to residence and age.
Since last Thursday wheit we discussed this clause I have studied clause 29, I have read several books and I have tried1 to find parallel legislation-legislation which would mean that in this country side by side we will have British subjects entitled to vote, and also British subjects who will be denied the right to vote. Nowhere can I find such legislation. Although, Mr. 'Chaiirman, I am sure you have read a good deal of history I do not think that you have ever

encountered an instance of such legislation in any history of the world. The only instance which comes anywhere near this piece of legislation is the laws passed under the Roman Empire, when the people were distributed into three classes: The Roman citizens, the slaves, and the foreigners. The foreigners, if you refer to that legislation, you will find included not only people but also animals not indigenous to Italy. When, for instance, elephants were introduced during the first battles against Pyrrhus they were immediately designated by the legislature of Ithe Roman Empire as foreigners, when strange birds from Asia were introduced into Italy they were classed as foreigners; when wild beasts from Africa were brought back to Rome by pro-consuls they also were classified as foreigners. Is this Government going to carry ns back to the time of the Roman Empire? Are we in the country, which is supposed to have a progressive and democratic policy, going back to the policy which has been rejected by every other country in the world? I do not believe that onr people will endorse such a policy.
Now, one word and I will conclude. The President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell) made a very strong appeal to this committee to-night, and he based it on legislation introduced by the Hearst Government. I have only this to say in reply. The Hearst Government after introducing that legislation went to the people-and the President of the Privy Council knows what happend to that government. If he takes his precedent from the Hearst Government, he may at the next election meet the same fate as the ministers of that government did when they appealed to the people of the province. Wc do not want as a precedent for legislation in this House legislation passed by defunct governments; we want live legislation; we want legislation that secures the rights of the people. And I think the amendment brought in by the [DOT]hon. member from Lambton is an amendment that ought to be adopted by the majority of this committee.

Subject to the insertion of a few words, to which I shall refer in a moment, I desire to endorse the amendment of the hon, member for West Lambton, and I think that strong reasons can be given in support of it. The Minister of Militia in opposing the amendment based his case upon, shall I say the sacred character of the Naturalization Act? He said that this amendment was an attempt virtually to amend the Naturaliza-

tion Act; thereupon he proceeded in the very warmest manner to defend the ten-year clause in that Act. He said that ten years was not too long; it was a perfectly good clause; it was all right-. But he forgot something. He forgot that his two colleagues, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) and the President of the Council (Mr. Rowell) said that it was all wrong. The other evening these hon. gentlemen told us that they were instituting negotiations with the British Government with a view to trying to get that provision Changed. I put the question directly to the Minister of Justice when he was speaking .of the negotiations in general terms. I said: tell us what was the object of these negotiations; what was it you wanted? Well, he said, the ten-year clause is capable of alteration. I said: then you want to reduce that period? Yes, that was it. So they are negotiating- and the Minister of Militia is a party to it- to get a change in the Naturalization Act as respects the ten-year clause. Yet the Minister of Militia bases his whole objection to the amendment on the ground that the ten-year clause is absolutely correct and proper. Now, that clause has caused a grievance. The Minister of Justice admitted that it was a grievance; the President of the Council admitted that it was a grievance. If it was not a grievance, why were these hon. gentlemen trying to get the clause changed? There is, then, according to their statement, not mine, a grievance existing under that ten-year clause. The Minister of Militia does not see it. He says it is a splendid clause; ten years is not too long; he almost talked as if he would like to make it twenty. But while he says-ten years is not too long, the Minister of Justice and the President of the Council say that it is too long, and that they are doing their best to have it changed. Well now, the Minister of Justice,, the President of the Council and myself had a little friendly conversation as to the possibilities of getting that provision changed by negotiation. The Minister of Justice and the President of the Council, admitting the grievance, thought we should endeavour by negotiation with the British Government to obtain a reduction of the ten-year term which my hon. friend, the Minister of Militia -says is admirable. Well, I did not think that the prospect of getting it changed was a bright one. It ie important to bear in mind Chat both the Minister of Justice and the President of the Council considered that there was -a grievance in
the present condition of affairs; the Minister of Militia took the opposite view; and I have to make up my mind as to which of these views is correct. If they are entering upon negotiation with the British Government in order to remove this grievance, I am bound to believe that the Minister of Militia has been away for a while and is not informed of what is going on in the Government of which he is a member.
I do not see any prospect of remedying this grievance in the way that the Minister of Justice and the President of the Council have suggested. I know the delay that takes place in connection with such negotiations. It is hard to get decisions from a Government; then after you get your decision you have to introduce an Act of Parliament. As I said in the previous discussion, the Naturalization Act is virtually a treaty between the Imperial Government and the Governments of the overseas dominions, and it is not likely that you can bring about any change until negotiations have been had between the parties. We all know how slow things of that kind are in coming to a finality; months, probably years, will pass before you can get a remedy for the grievance which the Minister of Justice and the President of the Council say exists. Then my hon. friend (Mr. Pardee) comes in and says:	since we
are not likely to get the remedy for that grievance in the way these Ministers suggest, why can we not remedy it ourselves? We do not need to amend the Naturalization Act. We cannot by any Act of our own create an Imperial citizenship, but we can create a Canadian citizenship for the purposes of this Act. If there are honest people in this country who ought to have a vote but who are disqualified from voting by reason of that ten-year provision, tihent I say that while we cannot alter the Act as respects Imperial citizenship we can by our own Act declare the terms and conditions upon which we will apply a remedy of our own. And the remedy is this; that for the purposes of this Act, that is, for the purpose of voting and for no other purpose, these persons shall be qualified to be naturalized upon, the terms and conditions which existed in Canada before the passing of this Imperial Naturalization Act. What is wrong about that? That is not an amendment to the Naturalization Act. An amendment to the Naturalization Act would affect the question of Imperial citizenship.

Will the hon. member
say that a man who was in Canada for

twenty or thirty years prior to 1914 but *made no attempt to become a British citizen should be placed on the same footing with regard to the franchise as the man who became a British citizen during that period?
Well, I am afraid that my hon. friend is luring me into a broader discussion than I desire to undertake.

The amendment proposed by the member for West Lambton is that any man who has been in Canada and who has the qualifications, whether or not [DOT]he ever applied for British citizenship, should be a voter under this Act.

Well, I do not think
that the question whether one has applied or not makes very much difference. If my hon. friend wants a general declaration of my views on the franchise, while I do not want to go into such a br*ad question, let me say this: there is a troublesome and embarrassing question out in British Columbia regarding Asiatics. I confess that it is an embarrassing situation, and I do not wish at the moment, to express any opinion about it. But subject to that, and expressing no opinion about that, I say I believe that every person who is prepared to take the oath of allegiance, who has lived in Canada the necessary time, who has acted the part of a good citizen, and who wants to become naturalized, to become a citizen of Canada, by all means should be allowed to do so. As for disfranchising those who have been British subjects, that- is another feature of the Act; the terms that have been used by various speakers in condemnation of it are not too strong. But that is getting away from the amedment, to which I wish to confine myself.
First, I say, there is a grievance. We will put aside what the Minister of Militia said. He was away; he did not know what was going on; he did not know these negotiation about which the Minister of Justice ad the President of the Privy Council have told us. These hon. gentleme say that there is undoubtedly a grievance; that many worthy people in this country are going to be deprived of the opportunity to vote because of the misfortune of the Naturalization Act, and they propose to take up negotiations which may occupy some considerable time. Now, my proposal is, not that we shall attempt by any Act of our own to give to these people an Imperial naturalization; that we cannot do. But what I propose and what the member for West Lambton proposes is that for all the purposes of this Act, that is for the purpose of voting, those persons who have a grie-

vance shall, upon going to a judge and taking the oath of allegiance-that is not in the amendment, but these are the words I would like to see inserted; I take it that the member for West Lambton means that -these people, I say, who are disqualified by the operation of the Naturalization Act, shall have the right, upon proving that they are qualified by residence and otherwise to vote as citizens of Canada. That is what the amendment means and that is what I support.
Mr. TWEED IE': The argument which has been advanced tiy my hon. friend (Mr. Fielding) involves the question of our enalbling all people oif alien enemy origin who resided in Canada the necessary length of time prior to 1914 to be enfranchised under the present law.
It seems to me that the gist of the whole argument was suggested Iby the hon. gentleman who asked the question in regard to those people who had resided in this country thirty and forty years. I know of many instances of that throughout Western Canada. The period may not be so long, but there are men there who have lived in the Dominion ten, twelve, twenty-five years, who have never become naturalized. British citizenship, I think, is. one of the greatest blessings which any person can enjoy, and if there has been any fault in our country ini the past, it has (been the fault that all Governments in this country have held the queistion of citizenship at too slight a value. If those people who have lived in this country refused to make application for their naturalization papers when the required time had elapsed, are we going to set aside the principle of our citizenship simply in order to place those people on the voters' list? If they did not in that period appreciate their citizenship, there is no just ground upon which they can complain of the attitude of the Government if we do not pass sbme speedy, hasty legislation in order that they may enjoy the franchise at the next election. If they themselves were so inconsiderate of their rights during that long period, why should we now worry over the rights >and privileges which they seek to enjoy? -
Various matters in connection with the right to exercise the franchise in this country have been discussed, and as was pointed out by the hon. member for Gape Breton South (Mr. Butts) in connection with the administration of the affairs of the province of Nova Scotia, the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen'si (Mr. Fielding) who stands here to-night and asks us to extend

the franchise to the Germans, Austrians1, Bulgarians and Turks* who have resided in this country three years or more, is the very same hon. gentleman who deprived some twenty-five or thirty or iforty thousand good British subjects of the franchise in 'Nova Scotia while he was premier of that province. Did he manifest any interest in those who were good, true British subjects? I cannot for my part understand the change of heart to which he gives expressions tonight when he deliberately took the franchise from British subjects' when they were enjoying it, because they were working for a Government which was of a different political faith from.his own.
As regards the amendment of the hon. member for Lambton West ('Mr. Pardee), any man who has any pride in British citizenship and in his country should vote down that amendment, and let those people abide their time subject to the laws of this country.

'I am going to ask my hon. friend (Mr. Tweedie) a question. 'Supposing that all he has said regarding my action in the matter of a franchise in Nova Scotia were as true as it is untrue, what bearing would it have on the discussion? What reason does it give for anything that is said here to-night?

The bearing which it
has is what 3 pointed out, namely, that I cannot understand the attitude of any hon. gentleman who will deprive any British subject of the franchise, and who will at this time manifest such great distress on account o,f Germans, Austrians, Bulgarians, Turks or any other alien enemy who resides in this country. The point which II wish to make is, that he wishes to set at naught or treat lightly the great benefits of British citizenship in this country, and on that point I take issue with the hon. gentleman. I have no doubt that he is sincere in the views which he sets forth. I am equally sincere in the views I set forth; and I believe the great mass of the people of this country who enjoy the- franchise do not want alien enemies rushed in so that they may enjoy those privileges simply because they have resided in this country for a period of three years.

Much of the discussion to-night has not been about alien enemies; it has been about the disfranchisement .by this legislation of British subjects, persons declared by the law of the Empire, by the law of Canada, to be British subjects.

The hon. member (Mr. Fielding) knows perfectly well that the Minister of Militia, who is in charge of this Bill, pointed out, clearly and in a manner which is beyond contradiction, that this is not a Bill for the disfranchisement of any person who enjoys the franchise of this country; it simply does not include a certain class of people to whom he referred. But the hon. member (Mr. Fielding) now endeavours to divert the issue from this amendment, and the point- of this amendment is that it intends to naturalize Austrians and Germans and others, who have lived in this country for a period of three years before the year 1914, some of whom perhaps have lived in this country for thirty or forty years. I am not entering into the general discussion as regards the clause, but I say that I am absolutely opposed to giving those people the right to exercise the franchise at the next election in this country simply because they lived in this country three years.
Mr. FIELDING; I_ have only one other question. I am assuming now that my hon. friend is a rational being.
I am.

I aim speaking courteously. Will he tell me why he supposes that these people who for forty years have been in Canada with no desire to have the vote, are suddenly going to be seized with a desire to vote?

I do not know. It was the hon. gentleman who was asked before distinctly if he divided them into two classes, those who had resided here for a period of three years and those who had resided here for ten, twelve, twenty-five or forty years. As to the first, if they came to this country from Germany, or Austria, or Bulgaria, or Turkey, or any other alien enemy country, he must know just as well as I do that after such a short period of separation from their mother country, when the war broke out, they must have had an attachment for their mother country, and that during the period of the war, if they ever had any slight attachment for Great Britain or the Dominion of Canada, that must have been wiped out- by the stand of Germany or their native country in the war. As regards the other class, if they did not respect and value their citizenship in this country enough to apply for and secure naturalization and enjoy the franchise, they are not worthy of consideration at the pre-

sent time under the circumstances, and in view of the struggle through which this country has passed.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Tweedie) has become very vehement over this matter. Perhaps he might say what his Government did not very many years ago. May I refer to Orders in Council which have been passed regarding the very subject upon which this amendment is founded? If the hon. member will take the trouble to look up Orders in Council Nos. 2552 and 2948, a portion of which have been quoted here tonight, he will find that the Government, when they passed one of those Orders in Council, had exactly this class of citizens in mind, and they said to themselves:	It
is not a fair proposition to disfranchise these men who have been many years in this country and believe themselves to be British subjects, but who cannot prove that they have their full naturalization, and we will give them the vote. There is no doubt about that. The letter was quoted here to-night; it has been sent for now, and if I get it will read it. Surely the hon. gentleman cannot deny that if they have resided in Canada for three years prior to 1914 and from 1914 to 1920, they have been here for ten years, which is as much as the Naturalization Act itself calls for. Surely that is sufficient to entitle them to vote under the Act. Order in Council No. 2552 reads in part as follows:
The minister observes further that many persons of alien enemy origin who came to Canada many years ago, during infancy, and have grown up believing themselves to be British slbjects, now that questions of nationality are being carefully scrutinized, find it impossible to show that they have become British subjects, although they have voted and held municipal positions for many years.
That is, they are merely naturalized by reason of the great number of years that they have resided in this country.
Many others believe that they became British subjects through the naturalization of their parents, but they are unable to prove it because the records are not available.

This is being done for a political purpose, and it will have one effect and one only, and that is to keep open a wound that should be healed and that will not make the country united.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
If this amendment has done nothing else, it has exposed the pretensions of hon. gentlemen opposite as regards the principle that governs them in matters of the franchise. 1 have sat_ in this House for many years and, particularly in recent years, I have heard it urged times without number from across the floor that naturalization and the franchise go hand in hand, and that it is a crime to take away the franchise from any person who enjoys naturalization. They have argued that the franchise is founded upon naturalization, rests there, is part and parcel of naturalization, and cannot be divorced therefrom. It is true they carried it too far. There was no truth in the doctrine at all. It is true that while they argued in favour of that doctrine they themselves were parties to the disfranchisement of half the citizens of this country and resisted the enfranchisement of that half. It is true they had no sincerity when they so argued, but at least that was the rock they believed they stood on; and on that they made their fight. Where do they stand now? They look over this country and find a class of our population whom they would like to see given the vote. Why they would like to have those people vote it is for them to say and for us only to conjecture; and I would conjecture that they believe they would get the support of those people. Do they say it is because they are naturalized citizens? Is it because the franchise is necessary, appurtenant to, and cannot be separated from, naturalization? Oh no ! They are on other ground altogether. They have forgotten all of their preachings of the last four or five years and now tell us that even though these people are not naturalized it is the duty of the Government to give them the vote. And the hon. member for Lambton West (Mr. Pardee) reads an Order in Council which he says is being repealed by this Bill and which had the effect of enabling the naturalization of certain people in this country who had

lived for many years and who possibly through a technicality were not in a position to comply with the requirements. Any person who came in under that Order in Council had to assume all the obligations of citizenship in this country before he could be naturalized or enjoy any of the benefits of naturalization. Is that the case with this amendment?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is? Would any man or woman who came and sought the vote under that amendment be bound by any of the obligations of citizenship?
I admit that I should have added, "on their taking the oath of allegiance." With the consent of the committee I now desire to do so.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: However, what I am discussing is the Act itself. I say that under the War-time Elections Act no citizen of any country hut Canada had the right to vote.	,

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If hon. members desire to raise any question regarding the way in' which the Act was carried out they may do so, as they did before, and again they will he beaten. But if they are capable of turning their minds to the point at issue I shall address them. The War-time Elections Act gave the franchise to British subjects and to no man or woman who was not a British subject. Citizens of the United States came to Canada and enlisted here; the War-time Elections Act was passed, and not one of these .pen was given the vote.
They did vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Not an hon. member on . the other side-and they are sitting in this House tonight-rose in his place and suggested that any American' citizen or the citizen of any other country should have the vote by that Act, even though they were at the time fighting in the defence of this country. Now, Sir, let me ask you: Does it not occur to you as rather curious than hon. gentlemen opposite should see an Act passed, at a time when the citizens of another country had enlisted to serve this country in its defence in Europe, and never suggest that those men should have the vote? They never suggested that those men should be enfranchised, because they were not our citizens; but now they lopk abroad and see Germans Austrians, Bulgars and others who are not our citizens, and they are most solicitous in their behalf, being exceedingly anxious that they should be given the vote. Surely, Mr. Chairman-
That is Toryism.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I put my Toryism
against the Liberalism of hon. gentlemen opposite.
You will have to come to it.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I address this particularly to the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe), because none needs it more. Surely if there ever was a time *when the doors of the franchise could be opened to the citizens of a country otheT than our own it was the time when this country in its peril was being defended by citizens of other countries who had sworn allegiance for that purpose. Surely they might have been admitted to the franchise.

That was never asked for, that was never included in our law. But now hon. gentlemen rise in the House and ask that men who have never sought citizenship in Canada, who, for all we know do not want citizenship in the British Empire and who have not been burdened with a single obligation of citizenship, be granted the rights of citizenship-that the doors be thrown wide open and that these people may be given the ballot the same as citizens of this country. In what position are hon. gentlemen placed? For years they have sought to malign the election laws of Canada on the ground that you never could divorce citizenship from the ballot; If this amendment has done nothing more it has shown that there has been no principle inspiring the Opposition in their antagonism to former election laws any more than there has been in their antagonism to this ; and if this discussion has done nothing more it at least has served a purpose in one respect: it has shown that the only rule which governs hon. gentlemen opposite in matters of franchise is a pretty shrewd conjecture as to what class of people in this country is likely to support themselves.	.

If the Government is
really sincere in desiring to implement the promise made by the right hon. the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) it wmulh be quite possible for them to ensure that the [DOT]people under discussion to-night should be given the vote and proper naturalization. I am one of those who argued, and argued very sincerely, that the vote ought to go with citizenship. I believe that yet. I am going to support the amendment of my hon. friend from West Lambton, and I shall do it for this reason: If it is logical for this Government to take the vote away from British subjects in one ease, it is just as logical to give it to people who are not technically British subjects. The hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) states that there is a grievance. That there is a grievance is, I think, admitted by responsible members of the Government. That is amply proven. The Prime Minister himself has said that he considers these people have a grievance. That is proven in different ways. It was proven by making provision in 1917 by means of Orders iri Council which were designed to provide for the naturalization of these people in a proper way. It was proven by the Prime Minister's speeches at the Peace Conference and it was proven by the attitude of the President of the

Privy Council when he backed up the Prime Minister in that matter. It was proven the other night by the Minister of Justice when he admitted there was a grievance. It was even proven by the Acting Solicitor General although he takes a different attitude to-night. To-night he is willing to withdraw what he said in the debate in 1919. To-night he thinks that these people who have been here longer than ten years should not be giv-en the vote; and yet in the debate of 1919 after I had made an argument to the effect that we should have made it possible for these people to become technically Canadians by giving them naturalization the Acting Solicitor General made some observations. I should add that I had moved an amendment to the effect that the clause should be amended as follows:
That such person is the subject of a country which at the passing- of this Act was at war with His Majesty, provided that such subject was permanently resident in Canada on the 4th day of August in the year one thousand nine hundred and nine.
The effect of that was that a person who had lived in Canada for ten years should be given the right of securing naturalization. I thought that amendment was reasonable and it was reasonable at that time to the Acting Solicitor General, because he said:
I confess that the amendment does1 not appear to be unreasonable but I would like to have an opportunity of considering whether or not it would be deemed a radical change from the provisions of the Imperial Act, and as there are several other elements in the proposal which I shall have to consider, I would ask that the matter stand over until some future occasion in order that I might look into it.
He based his objection not upon the same ground as he has to-night but merely upon the fact that the amendment might conflict with the Imperial Naturalization Act. We have this expression of opinion from the Prime Minister, the President of the Privy Council and the Minister of Justice, that there is a grievance here to be remedied. If this amendment cannot be accepted, and if the Government is sincere in all it has said, I would like to make the suggestion that I made the other night and that is that this House re-enact the old Canadian Naturalization law and that it have force until such time as the Imperial Naturalization law may be altered. That is surely a fair suggestion. It conforms entirely to the views of the Government if they desire to give these people the franchise and naturalization. The answer made to that the other night was that they did not wish to have a
dual naturalization law. But you have that in effect now. You had it for some time in the past and you actually have it to-day. As a matter of fact, while you speak of giving these people of enemy alien origin the Imperial naturalization, after you have successfully completed- your negotiations with the British Government, they will not get Imperial naturalization any way. Take men who came from Germany, Bulgaria, Austria or Turkey; if they have Canadian naturalization to-day that is all they can get. The members of the Government know that to be the fact because we know that some of these men have made application for an Imperial naturalization certificate and they have been refused. If they are refused that now, what chance have others of getting the Imperial Naturalization certificate?
I say, none at all. Then, under the circumstances, if it is conceded that these men are worthy of naturalization-and I am not asking on behalf of anybody else-they still have to come before the judge. If you enact the old Canadian naturalization law it is not a matter of throwing the doors wide open to everybody in the country; it means that they still have to go before the judge *and prove that they are worthy of naturalization;. If they prove that they should be given Canadian naturalization-and as I said the other night that would serve the purpose in nine hundred and ninety-nine cases out of a thousand-give them Canadian naturalization. That is what they want; they are Canadians first, last, and ail the time; and it is no reflection upon their patriotism to say that Canadian citizenship probably appeals much more to them than Imperial citizenship-I should think it would to everybody in this country. As far as I am concerned I would like' to make that suggestion in all sincerity and good faith to the Government. Why could it not be possible, at this very session of the House-because it need not be debated at length to re-enact that Ganad' an naturalization law. Under that Act these men can become naturalized and the vote will necessarily flow from such naturalization. I should like to know from the Government what possible objection there can be to that? I think that would be the preferable and the better way, because then they would be British subjects and the franchise will flow out of that fact. I ask again what objection can there be to it? That is the best way, but if that way cannot be followed I assuredly will vote for the amendment of the hon. member for Lambton in order to do justice to these people.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must point out to the hon. member (Mr. Cahill) that it is not sufficient for him to rise and remain standing. If he desires to prevent or delay the putting of the question, he must continue the debate.

I thought it was customary for the chair to ask for order, and I was waiting for order to be restored. It may be the rule that you must do more than stand on your feet and wait for order to be restored.
Order, order.

I doubt very much, Mr. Chairman, if there is any rule defining how fast a man shall speak or how much time he shall occupy in debate. If hon. members opposite are not anxious to get away from here in a great hurry, they can very well continue as they are doing now and they will get all the entertainment they are looking for.
Before the clause carries I want to draw the attention of the Government to the fact that this country at the present time is in worse need of people than of anything else. I think the Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Calder) will agree with me on that. And yet this clause wall work directly against immigration. When people come to a country they come to make new homes, to better their condition, and to be-

come citizens. But after men and women have been in this contry for forty, fifty and in some cases sixty years enjoying the rights of citizenship, and find that by an Act of this Government they are precluded from exercising the franchise, I submit that the *Government of the day could do nothing better calculated to work a great hardship on our taxpayers than by passing this Act, which will exclude for the future not only Germans, Bulgarians, and Turks, but American and British subjects-the very people that we want; because if the Government juggle with them as they did last year by passing legislation under Which they can send British subjects out of the country-a piece of legislation that was rushed through this House without any consideration-	.
Order.

There seem to be several *chairmen calling for order, Mr. Chairman.
I do not know whether they are assuming to undertake the duties of the Chair or not. This very measure juggling with the franchise will be the means of keeping good prospective citizens out of this country. *There is no question about that. When my hon. friend from West Calgary (Mr. Tweedie) says that a man who has been in this country for twentydive or thirty years without asking for naturalization should not have it, the reflection is not on the alien, it is on the Canadian people. There must be something radically wrong with Cana-dianism when men and women will live in this country for thirty years and fail to ask for citizenship. When my hon. friends the other day introduced the question of education and urged that we do. something for our foreign immigrants, I thought they were taking the Tight course, and I think so still. But it is the business of the Government and of every citizen not to attempt to juggle with the votes of these immigrants as has been done in the past.
When it is said that this Act cannot be changed, I would ask my hon. friend the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell) what course are the Ontario Government adopting in this matter? Are they being guided by the Naturalization Act? Not at all. Every province makes its own franchise; and surely the Dominion Government, has no less power than the governments of the provinces. We have a much greater responsibility than the provinces- a responsibility to every immigrant, and it is a responsibility that we should not treat as lightly as it is being treated here tonight by hon. Ministers of the Crown in
trying to pass this legislation. One minister stated that the franchise had been passed last year without opposition. In 1918. my first session, the first measure I spoke on was the Franchise Bill. I was in favour of woman suffrage, but I was opposed to having it tied up to the War Time Elect'ons Act. It was explained that it could not be done in any other way, and I accepted it for that reason because I wanted women to have the vote. Hon. members get up and say that everyone on this side of the House was opposed to woman suffrage. One minister says there was no opposition. Well, he has apologized for telling an untruth. Another minister says he was reading from an Act submitted to the legislature of Ontario; and he must admit that- he is stating an untruth. They treat this matter in that way, they pay no attention to it any further than to get this Act in such shape that they can carry off another election. They have no more regard for the country, they have no more regard for citizenship, they have no more regard for what is decent and honest than to simply say:	Give us this
Franchise Act, we will force it through anyway, so that we may have a chance to get back again to the Treasury benches. The attention seems to be so good that I think I will desist; otherwise if my hon. friends want to prolong the discussion I am quite willing that they ishould do so. However, I just rose to go on record as protesting against this Act going through in this manner. So perhaps in future my hon. friends will have a little more patience.

Before the clause carries I wish to emphasize again the situation created by the answer given to me tonight by the Acting solicitor General regarding the case I brought before the House. It was the case of a gentleman who came to this country from France thirty years ago, with his wife and his son who was seven years old. After a while he got his naturalization papers, and, of course, by the operation of the law his wife and son became British subjects. When the war broke out in August, 1914, the son took the first boat for France, he fought for five years, and he was decorated with the Military Medal and the Legion of Honour. His mother, who resided in Montreal, took part in all the war charities; that is she was practically the head of the charity organizations in that city, and she did such good work that she also was decorated by the Government of France. The mother and the son had both voted in the election of



1917; they had the right to vote. Now, according to the interpretation given by the Acting Solicitor General, this woman, who during five years cared for the relatives of those who went to the front, and her son who during five years risked his life and was wounded for the cause of civilization, will be deprived of their votes unless they will submit to the humiliation-I insist on this word-the humiliation of going before a judge and submitting to an inquiry regarding their loyalty and probably being cross<-examined by one of the government officials; and yet if the husband of this woman and the father of this boy had come from the slums of Chicago or had been a Mexican desperado they would not be obliged to submit to this humiliation. I appeal to the fairness of members of the committee. Is it fair that this woman and this boy who did more than their duty during the war should not be entitled to vote without going through this procedure, while the eon of a man from Mexico or of a man from the slums of Chicago, who probably did nothing during the war, is entitled to vote without going through it. I submit that any member who does not realize the unfairness of this situation is either blinded by political eagerness, or, non compos mentis.

I wish to protest against this clause being carried in its present form. On Thursday last I put the following question to the minister in charge of the Bill:
Will the minister be kind enough to tell me what good reason there is and what good purpose will be served by compelling these British subjects to travel miles from their homes to obtain certificates?
The minister answered, if answer it can be termed:
Under this Bill as drawn it is provided that a person who has become a British subject by operation of law, in order to vote, shall obtain a certificate from a judge. That certificate is not for the purpose of identity, as my hon. friend from George Etienne Cartier suggested a few moments ago; it is for the purpose of satisfying the judge that the woman has such qualifications that in any event, though she may be a British subject by operation of law, she would be entitled to naturalization.
He admits that these people who are compelled to make applications are British subjects. Clause 29 says, in respect of the qualification of a voter:
A voter is one who
(a)	is a British subject by birth or naturalization ; and,
(b)	is of the full age of twenty-one years; and,

(c)	has ordinarily resided in Canada for at least twelve months and in the electoral district wherein such person seeks to vote for at least two months immediately preceding the issue of the writ of election.
Under this clause it is noit claimed That these people who are compelled to travel many miles at inconvenience to themselves and their families to appear before a judge and obtain this certificate are not British subjects. The law says that ito have a vote you must he a British subject. Why, then, are these people compelled to go to this unnecessary trouble to obtain a certificate? If the reason is good, why did the minister noit tell the committee what that reason was? Later, the minister said:
The amendment I have submitted meets with the approval of the Government and it is the desire that it be passed.
It seems to me that the Government should be in a position to tell the committee and the country what reason they have for insisting that these people who are British subjects should be compelled to obtain these certificates. It has been suggested that the reason is political; that the motive is not what it should be. If that is the case, I will make my remarks very brief. I am sorry that the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Calder) is not in his seat, because he knows the conditions in Saskatchewan even better than I do. He must know that if this provision is carried into the law thousands of people in the western provinces will, in effect, at any rate, be disfranchised. If that is the intention of the Government, then this proposed legislation is worse than the War-time Elections Act. Under the Wartime Elections Act the Government went out and disfranchised people by what I would term front-door methods, but in this case, they give the franchise with one hand and take it away with the other; instead of using front door methods they are going in the back door and depriving these people of the right to the franchise.
I have nothing to say on behalf of the newcomers to this country or against the ten-year residence clause as contained in the Naturalization Act. Taking into consideration the promise made by the Prime Minister, I have, however, something to say on behalf of the people who are already in this country, who came here at our invitation. We went so far as to send our immigration officers into their country to invite them to come here and it seems to me that if we want to build up in this country a united citizenship, that is a mighty poor way to go about it. I think that gvery hon. member looked upon the resolution intro-

duced a few days ago by the member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) in respect to the education of the foreign-born in this country as a good resolution. You can say all you like along the lines suggested in that resolution, but if you treat newcomers to this country as we propose to treat them under the terms of this Bill, you will undo everything you do in every other way. I dissociate myself from anything that may have been said on behalf of foreigners in this country. No one from this group has been making a plea for foreigners. These people are Canadian citizens, British subjects in this country, but for some reason this Government has seen fit to bring down a Bill that will in effect disfranchise subjects who are entitled to the vote.
It had to come out.

Well, I hope it does not make my hon. friend siok; it has not had that effect on me. When the question of

extending the franchise to women iwas before the House, my friend will admit, certain hon. gentlemen opposite from Quebec objected to the extension of the franchise to women, and that, I believe is the attitude generally of that province. I am not going to quarrel with the people of Quebec for taking that attitude if they choose to take it. A great deal can be said both for and against the extension of the franchise to women, but I think I am stating what is correct when I say that a strong feeling was manifested in this House by certain members from Quebec against extending the franchise to women, which feeling Was not manifested, at least to the same extent, by members from any other province. It was their privilege to express that disapproval if they wished to do so, but it seems slightly inconsistent on the part of those hon. gentlemen who objected generally to the extension of the franchise to women to show now such solicitude on behalf of women of alien enemy origin who happen to reside in this country. Those who give this bill careful study and consideration will see in this clause certain safeguards which we should have in this legislation in order to protect those people who are entitled to the franchise. We have been entirely too slack in that regard in times past; we have held our franchise entirely too cheaply, and the safeguards which are inserted are no more than are right under existing circumstances. True, the war is over, but the people of this country have not yet forgotten and will not forget for many years to come that there was a war. They are still suffering from the losses which many of them have sustained in that war, and it is in the interest of all concerned that there should be a period of probation, so to speak, before certain people are taken into full citizenship.	*i
